items.title: Mental health and workforce participation in India: A gendered analysis.
items.authors: Shah FM, Husain Z, Dutta M, Datta SS.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Depression adversely affects labor market outcomes globally. In low- and middle-income countries like India, where informal employment is prevalent and mental health services are limited, poor mental health may be associated with substantial economic disadvantages. However, large-scale empirical evidence remains limited, especially on gendered patterns.

sections.heading: Aim
sections.text: This study examines the association between depression and employment among midlife adults (ages 45-60) in India and explores how this relationship varies by gender and socio-economic status.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Using nationally representative data from the Longitudinal Ageing Study in India (Wave 1), we analyze 27,092 individuals reporting current working status. Depression is measured using the Composite International Diagnostic Interview-Short Form via both continuous scores and threshold-based cutoffs. To account for potential endogeneity, we employ a control function approach and probit-2SLS models, with parental psychiatric history and number of confidants as instruments. Gender-disaggregated and subgroup analyses cover income and education levels.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Depression is associated with lower likelihood of employment, even at subclinical levels. The gender gap in employment is narrow among the depressed; the pattern is consistent with distress-driven employment and constrained agency.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: The counterintuitive narrower gender disparity among the depressed-largely driven by disadvantaged women-contrasts with conventional expectations about India's labor market. Integrating gender-sensitive mental health support into employment and social protection programs, even for subclinical cases, may be relevant to protect vulnerable workers, reduce economic insecurity, and promote equitable workforce participation.

items.title: Psychiatric facets of Wilson's disease: A case series.
items.authors: Bhat AK, Bhelonde K, Negi S.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Wilson's disease is a rare genetic syndrome characterised by multisystemic copper accumulation. Psychiatric symptoms are common and can present at any point in the course of the disease, often before clear neurological or hepatic signs are evident, thus creating diagnostic and therapeutic challenges.

sections.heading: Cases
sections.text: The following case series describes three male patients with a psychotic syndrome in the context of Wilson's disease, highlighting the diversity in possible etiologies, outcomes, and pharmacotherapy.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Psychiatrists must be aware of the differential diagnoses and safest treatment approaches as they often are the first point of contact for the patient with Wilson's disease.

items.title: A home-based video-supervised adapted physical activity program in adult women with anorexia nervosa: a pilot study.
items.authors: Genoux B, Guillaume S, Buis C, Bakouline MC, Bosson JL, Bétry C.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Anorexia nervosa is a severe mental disorder associated with high mortality and reduced quality of life. Adapted physical activity programs have shown promising results but have been developed primarily in inpatient settings. This pilot study aimed to assess the safety and satisfaction of a home-based adapted physical activity program delivered via videoconference in outpatient adult women with anorexia nervosa, and to generate preliminary data including initial uptake, session completion, and retention to inform a future randomized controlled trial.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: APAMAdom is a prospective, single-arm, non-randomized multicenter pilot study conducted in two specialized eating disorder centers within two French university hospitals (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT05803707). Adult women aged 18 to 60 years with anorexia nervosa and a body mass index below 18.5 kg/m² were eligible. The program consisted of 10 sessions including 8 weekly 45-minute adapted physical activity sessions delivered by qualified instructors via videoconference. Potential pre-to-post program changes in body weight, body composition, physical activity levels, exercise dependence, quality of life, and self-esteem were assessed. Results are reported descriptively, with pre-to-post program comparisons performed using a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: A total of 36 women were included (median age 33 [26-47] years, median body mass index 15.6 [14.7-16.8] kg/m², median disease duration 10 [4-17] years). The retention rate for the completion of the end-of-program visit was 63.9%. The initial uptake rate defined as the proportion of eligible participants (n = 66) who completed the first session, was 36.4%. Among enrolled participants, 13.9% (n = 5) completed all 10 sessions. One participant was withdrawn due to weight loss exceeding 5% of baseline body weight. Satisfaction was high, with 77.3% of the 22 respondents wishing to continue the program. Body weight, body composition, physical activity levels, and exercise dependence remained stable throughout the program, whereas medium effect sizes suggesting improvement in quality of life and self-esteem were observed (r = 0.40 and r = 0.36 respectively).

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: This pilot study provides real-world data for a home-based adapted physical activity program delivered by videoconference in adult women with anorexia nervosa, including estimates of initial uptake, session completion, and retention, together with a reassuring safety profile. The data generated also provide the foundation for the design of a future randomized controlled trial, for which quality of life is proposed as the primary outcome.

items.title: Does Neurobiological Evidence Support the Diagnostic Distinction Between Hoarding Disorder and OCD? A Critical Narrative Review of Genetic, Neuroimaging, and Neuropsychological Findings.
items.authors: Li J, Liu X, Li J.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Hoarding symptoms were long regarded as one dimension of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), but DSM-5 (2013) classified hoarding disorder (HD) as a separate diagnosis. This review asks whether neurobiological evidence, including studies published after the reclassification, adequately supports that decision.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This critical narrative review searched PubMed and Web of Science (January 2010 to July 2026, plus foundational studies found by citation tracing) and was structured according to the SANRA criteria. Genetic, neuroimaging, and neuropsychological evidence was judged against four questions: is hoarding a separable trait within OCD; do groups differ biologically on average; is any difference specific to hoarding; and can the evidence classify an individual patient?

sections.heading: Main findings
sections.text: Twin studies suggest that hoarding-related traits have a heritability of about 26%-48%, and one genome-wide association study reported an SNP-based heritability of 11%. These estimates come from different models and are not directly comparable; they are compatible with a heritable, polygenic trait but do not by themselves show a disorder-specific genetic architecture. A small number of PET, structural MRI, functional MRI, and EEG studies report differences associated with hoarding, including seven direct HD-OCD comparisons, but samples are small, diagnostic criteria vary, and findings have not converged. An exploratory computational study has compared genetic signals for the two phenotypes, but no direct comparison of risk variants exists. Neuropsychological findings were inconsistent: the most recent systematic review found no significant impairment on most cognitive tests in HD.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Current neurobiological evidence provides only supplementary, not definitive, support for the diagnostic distinction between HD and OCD. It points to group-level biological heterogeneity, but it does not establish a distinct etiology or individual-level diagnostic utility. Larger studies using standardized DSM-5 criteria and direct HD-OCD comparisons are needed.

items.title: Mitochondrial Quality Control and Apoptotic Thresholds in Major Depressive Disorder: A Structured Narrative Review.
items.authors: Hou C, Li Z, Niu D, Zou W.

sections.text: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is clinically heterogeneous, and many patients do not achieve sustained remission with monoaminergic treatments. Mitochondrial dysfunction has been associated with chronic stress, impaired synaptic function, altered cellular energetics, and neuronal vulnerability, but evidence concerning mitochondrial dynamics, mitophagy, redox imbalance, calcium signaling, and intrinsic apoptosis remains distributed across experimental systems. This structured narrative review integrates human brain and peripheral studies, patient-derived cellular evidence, animal models, and general cell biology. We propose the mitochondrial quality control-mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MQC-MOMP) threshold model as a conceptual framework, not an experimentally established disease mechanism. In this model, cumulative failure of mitochondrial repair and clearance may shift stress responses toward Bax/Bak-dependent MOMP and caspase activation. Human findings are largely associative and do not establish widespread mitochondria-driven neuronal apoptosis in living patients with MDD; mechanistic support is strongest in preclinical and cellular models. The framework therefore differs from prior topic-based reviews by organizing heterogeneous evidence according to evidence source, certainty, and proximity to clinical translation. Here we highlight testable priorities for biomarker validation, patient stratification, cell-type-resolved studies, longitudinal cohorts, and mechanism-based interventions.

items.title: Self-disgust and the body as a target in self-harm and suicidal behavior: A narrative review.
items.authors: Jelaga D, Belous M.
items.journal: PCN reports : psychiatry and clinical neurosciences

sections.text: Self-harm and suicidal behavior are commonly framed as failures of emotion regulation, yet the emotions that make the body the target of harm remain under-specified. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on self-disgust as a candidate mechanism in non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) and in suicidal ideation and behavior. Self-disgust is an aversive self-directed emotion organized around the appraisal of the self, and often the body, as revolting or contaminated. Cross-sectional studies consistently link self-disgust with NSSI, suicidal ideation, and suicide-risk scores, and qualitative accounts place it at the center of some suicidal crises. Longitudinal studies from China suggest it mediates reciprocal links between emotional abuse and suicidal ideation and a path from body-image concerns to NSSI. Two prospective studies testing different roles did not support them, and the only induction study of self-harm urges is equivocal. In some studies, self-disgust explains variance beyond depression and constructs of the interpersonal theory of suicide. Its boundaries with shame and self-criticism are contested, and, across disorders, associations shrink when other negative self-referential emotions are controlled for. The central proposal, that the contamination-and-elimination logic of disgust explains why distress is enacted on the body, builds on earlier suggestions and remains an untested hypothesis. On this hypothesis, self-disgust is an embodied emotion whose action tendency of cleansing and removal may correspond to the phenomenology of cutting and, in some people, to a wish to eliminate a self experienced as contaminated. Implications for assessment and intervention, which remain untested, are outlined with falsifiable predictions for research.

items.title: The Influence of Group Psychological Counseling Based on Positive Psychology on Transition Shock and Professional Identity Among Graduate Nursing Students.
items.authors: Zhang Y, Chen M, Wu S, Ying C.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: To investigate how group psychological counseling based on positive psychology affects transition shock, professional identity, and mental health among graduate nursing students.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This study adopted a quasi-experimental research design. Participants were full-time graduate nursing students who were undergoing clinical rotation internships at Lishui People's Hospital between January 2025 and December 2025. They were allocated non-randomly by original class into an observation group (n = 51) and a control group (n = 46). The control group received routine hospital business training and general guidance on nurse psychological development. The observation group received routine hospital business training plus a three-week structured group psychological counseling program based on positive psychology, delivered twice weekly for 120 minutes per session. Primary outcomes (transition shock and professional identity) and secondary outcomes (depressive and anxiety symptoms) were assessed at baseline (T0) and within one week after the intervention (T1) using the New Graduate Nurse Transition Shock Scale, the Nurse Professional Identity Scale, the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9), and the Generalized Anxiety Disorder Scale (GAD-7). Linear mixed-effects models were used to examine the interaction effects of time and group.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: At T1, the transition shock scale's overall score, each dimension's score, and the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 scores were all significantly lower in the observation group than in the control group, whereas the professional identity scale's overall score was significantly higher. For every outcome indicator, the time × group interaction effect was statistically significant (P < 0.05).

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: In this preliminary study, group psychological counseling based on positive psychology was associated with short-term alleviation of transition shock and negative emotions among graduate nursing students and short-term enhancement of their professional identity. These findings provide innovative psychological counseling strategies and preliminary empirical evidence for constructing an evidence-based and effective psychological support intervention for graduate nursing students.

items.title: Behavioural profiling of social and locomotor responses to repeated ketamine exposure in adult zebrafish.
items.authors: Gallas-Lopes M, Müller DV, Stahlhofer-Buss T, Bastos LM, Becker SZ, Bruck SM, Piato A, Herrmann AP.

sections.text: N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonists are used to model schizophrenia-related phenotypes, but behavioural responses to repeated ketamine exposure in zebrafish remain poorly characterized. Three independent experiments were conducted to evaluate the acute, repeated and sustained behavioural effects of ketamine in adult zebrafish. In Experiment I, fish received 10, 20 or 40 mg l^-1 ketamine daily for 5 days and were tested in the social preference test (SPT) and open tank test (OTT) on days 1, 5 and 7, with re-exposure on day 7 after a 48 h washout. Experiments II and III assessed whether behavioural changes persisted following 5- or 14-day exposure, with testing 48 h after the final treatment. Ketamine reduced social interaction and increased locomotor activity in the SPT on all days and increased rotational behaviour in the OTT on days 1 and 5. Measured responses did not progressively increase across test sessions, and most outcomes did not differ from controls 48 h after the final exposure in Experiments II and III. The results characterize the acute, concentration-dependent behavioural profile of ketamine in adult zebrafish and define the temporal window over which it is detectable. These findings differ from rodent reports of sustained effects and motivate further investigation across species.

items.title: Examining smartphone-assessed executive function metrics and intrinsic resting-state functional connectivity in depression.
items.authors: Heckel JM, Clouse A, Klemballa D, Hernandez J, Park J, Leow AD, Ajilore OA, Bernard JA, Walther S, Mittal VA, Shankman SA, Letkiewicz AM.

sections.text: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is a common and costly mental health condition that is often associated with deficits in executive function. Smartphone applications ("apps") have emerged as promising methods for assessing mental health-related outcomes in individuals' daily lives that can detect changes that unfold over time. Although smartphone apps have been used to evaluate executive functioning in individuals with neurological conditions and in other mental health disorders, few studies have examined this in MDD. The present study tested whether smartphone-assessed executive function is (1) impaired in individuals with current MDD (cMDD; n = 30) relative to healthy controls (HC; n = 42) and (2) related to resting-state functional connectivity within cognitive control-related neural networks. For two weeks, participants completed a set-shifting (Trail Making Test, TMT-B) task on their smartphone. Participants with cMDD had significantly lower TMT accuracy (β = -0.24, p = 0.044) and greater variability in TMT accuracy (β = 0.25, p = 0.049) compared to HC. Resting-state analyses revealed that the association between TMT accuracy and connectivity between nodes of the dorsal attention network (bilateral intraparietal sulcus) was greater in HC than cMDD. The results extend previous laboratory-based findings by demonstrating that individuals with cMDD exhibit poorer mean-level smartphone assessed set-shifting performance and greater variability, along with altered set-shifting-related functional connectivity within the dorsal attention network. Smartphone-based assessments may offer a scalable and accessible approach for identifying executive function deficits in individuals with depression, which could be a useful tool for monitoring cognitive performance over time.

items.title: Substance use among helping professionals: rationalization and negotiation of professional identity.
items.authors: Lee GKW, Chan GH, Low YTA, Lo TW.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Given the scarce research on the drug use situation among helping professionals and the existing organizational structures that may affect them, this study explores how helping professionals in Hong Kong make sense of personal drug use and negotiate professional identity.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Narrative, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 15 helping professionals. Interviews were conducted in Cantonese, transcribed verbatim, and translated into English, prioritizing semantic equivalence for colloquialisms. Culturally specific terms were retained in parentheses with brief explanatory notes where needed. An interpretivist, reflexive thematic analysis was undertaken using NVivo.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Drug use served coping, social and/or sexual functions. Participants managed cognitive dissonance through compartmentalization, normalization and critiques of illegality, and by reframing lived experience as strengthening rapport and credibility with clients.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: While their drug use may not have directly caused impairment, their rationalization of behavior instead of disclosing it and seeking professional support suggests underlying organizational and institutional issues. Anticipated workplace sanctions and professional impairment discourse fostered concealment and delayed help-seeking. Therefore, rather than adopting a zero-tolerance governance approach, establishing clear practice-related thresholds and providing confidential, harm reduction-informed workforce supports may better protect these professionals' wellbeing and ensure service quality.

items.title: When severe violence becomes a script: a vulnerability-script integration model of media exposure and the form of psychosis-associated maternal filicide.
items.authors: Mohiyeddini C.

sections.text: When a publicized act of severe violence is followed by one that resembles it, the resemblance is often read as contagion. This paper argues that resemblance is weak evidence of influence and asks a narrower question: under what conditions can exposure to a publicized crime narrative shape the form of subsequent violence in a person whose antecedent state has already made such violence conceivable? The Vulnerability-Script Integration Model (VSIM) is developed for psychosis-associated maternal filicide. It is an organizing framework with an attached evidentiary protocol and three new propositions: antecedent vulnerability selects exposure as well as moderating its effect; exposure primarily shapes the form rather than the origin of violence; and media influence is inferred only from a dated post-exposure change in narrative-specific behavioral information (acquired or activated) that the documented antecedent state does not parsimoniously explain. The model specifies five functional stages, two moderators, a clinically defined and non-circular vulnerability construct, discriminant coding rules, a causal diagram with explicit estimands, and six predictions with stated classification, test, disconfirming, and inconclusive evidence. A closed, adjudicated case in which a court-tested claim of media scripting proved false illustrates the evidentiary rules. Clinical and reporting implications are framed as research questions.

items.title: Baseline cognitive insight moderates the efficacy of metacognitive training for psychosis: an individual participant data analysis.
items.authors: Goncalves A, Ochoa S, Moritz S, Gawęda Ł, Acuña V, König C, Lamarca M, Berna F.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Metacognitive Training (MCT) for psychosis is designed to target metacognitive processes, yet evidence for its effects on cognitive insight remains inconclusive, owing primarily to the limited methodological quality of available trials. A potential explanation lies in baseline heterogeneity, with a substantial proportion of participants presenting high baseline cognitive insight, thereby limiting observable change.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This study used harmonized individual participant data from the PERMEPSY database, including 614 participants with schizophrenia spectrum disorders from 13 international studies. Cognitive insight was assessed using the Beck Cognitive Insight Scale (BCIS), including Self-Reflectiveness (SR), Self-Certainty (SC), and a composite index (CI). Baseline moderation effects were examined using ANCOVA models with a continuous Group × Baseline interaction term, complemented by stratified ANOVAs to visualize the interaction pattern and estimate within-stratum effect sizes.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: ANCOVA models revealed significant Group × Baseline interactions across all BCIS dimensions, indicating that baseline cognitive insight moderated treatment response. Stratified ANOVAs yielded convergent results for SR and SC. Effect sizes followed a consistent gradient, with larger improvements observed among participants with lower baseline insight. Notably, 26.5% of participants already scored in the high-insight category at baseline, suggesting that ceiling effects may have partially obscured treatment effects at the group level in previous trials.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: MCT appears to improve cognitive insight, particularly among participants with greater baseline impairment. These findings suggest that baseline heterogeneity is a key determinant of MCT efficacy and may account for previously inconsistent results.

items.title: Legal awareness under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act and its associated factors among patients with substance use disorder: A cross-sectional analytical study.
items.authors: Barwa J, Udey B, Saini A, Singh R, Bhatia J, Singh J, Kumar A.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Substance use disorder (SUD) carries significant legal implications under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985 in India.

sections.heading: Objectives
sections.text: To assess awareness regarding legal provisions related to psychoactive substances and to identify factors associated with awareness among patients with SUD.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A hospital-based cross-sectional analytical study was conducted among 96 adult patients diagnosed with SUD attending the psychiatry outpatient department of a tertiary care hospital. Participants were recruited using consecutive sampling. Sociodemographic and clinical details were collected using a semi-structured proforma. Legal awareness was assessed using a structured 10-item questionnaire developed and content validated for this study based on provisions of NDPS Act. Multivariable logistic regression was used to explore factors independently associated with good/moderate legal awareness.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Overall, 79.2% of participants demonstrated poor awareness, while 20.8% had good/moderate awareness. Item-wise correct responses regarding procedural safeguards, rehabilitation provisions, quantity-based punishment, and bail restrictions ranged from 26.0% to 35.4%. Graduate-level education [adjusted odds ratio (AOR) = 22.76; 95% CI: 3.20-162.2; P < 0.01] and intention to quit substance use (AOR = 7.62; 95% CI: 1.01-57.27; P = 0.048) were independently associated with good/moderate legal awareness.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Legal awareness regarding the NDPS Act was poor among most treatment-seeking participants with SUD. Higher educational attainment and intention to quit were independently associated with better legal awareness.

items.title: Staff Experiences Delivering Hospital Outreach Post-Suicidal Engagement (HOPE) in a Regional Context: A Qualitative Study.
items.authors: Modderman C, Veresova M, McAleer R, Hanson L, Hemming L, Maude P, Spelten E.
items.journal: International journal of mental health nursing

sections.text: Suicide rates remain disproportionately high in regional Australia, where geographical, workforce and service-system constraints can limit access to post-suicidal care. This study explored staff experiences of delivering the Hospital Outreach Post-Suicidal Engagement (HOPE) program across three regional hospital sites in Victoria, Australia. Semi-structured individual interviews and one focus group were conducted with 16 HOPE staff, including nurses, peer workers, psychosocial support staff and allied health professionals. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, with reporting guided by the COnsolidated criteria for REporting Qualitative research (COREQ) checklist. Four themes were identified: regional influences on HOPE service delivery; adaptations to individual consumer needs; workforce capacity and teamwork; and HOPE's integration with the broader healthcare system. Staff valued HOPE's multidisciplinary and person-centred approach but identified barriers associated with geographical distance, infrastructure, workforce capacity and fragmented service pathways. The findings demonstrate how regional context shapes the delivery of post-suicidal care and highlight the importance of adequately resourced, flexible and integrated service models. These findings have implications for multidisciplinary HOPE practice, workforce planning and continuity of post-suicidal care across regional communities.

items.title: Effectiveness of LGBTQ targeted cognitive behavioral therapy on mental health outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis protocol.
items.authors: Chi JD, Yang Y, Wang SY, Nyhan K, Jackson SD.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Sexual and gender minority populations experience disproportionately high rates of mental disorders due, in large part, to their chronic exposure to stigma, discrimination, and minority stress. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an established evidence-based psychotherapy; however, conventional CBT was primarily developed among predominantly cisgender, heterosexual individuals and not often addresses identity-specific stressors relevant to LGBTQ individuals. Emerging adaptations of LGBTQ-affirmative CBT integrate components that affirm sexual and gender minority identities and target minority stress. Although the number of investigations testing such interventions has increased, evidence remains fragmented across studies. To our knowledge, no systematic review has examined the efficacy of LGBTQ targeted CBT on improving mental health outcomes.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: This systematic review aims to synthesize empirical evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating the effectiveness of LGBTQ targeted CBT interventions in reducing mental health symptoms among sexual and gender minority adults.

sections.heading: Materials and methods
sections.text: A comprehensive search will be conducted across PubMed, EMBASE, PsycINFO, the Cochrane Library, and Scopus, supplemented by gray-literature searches. Eligible studies include RCTs conducted on adults aged 18-65 and evaluating LGBTQ targeted CBT compared with usual care, waitlist, or active controls. Outcomes include depression, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, and substance use disorder symptom changes at post-intervention and follow-up. Data extraction and risk-of-bias assessment will be performed independently by two reviewers, with risk of bias assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool. Where feasible, meta-analyses using random-effects models in R will estimate standardized mean differences or risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals. Overall efficacy and potential moderators, such as intervention delivery mode and duration, will be investigated.

sections.heading: Expected contribution
sections.text: By consolidating the evidence base for LGBTQ targeted CBT, this review will clarify its efficacy, identify key intervention features associated with improved outcomes, and provide guidance for evidence-based mental health care for sexual and gender minority populations.

sections.heading: Prospero registration
sections.text: This protocol has been pre-registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO: CRD420251173207).

items.title: Fear Engrams are Formed in the Locus Coeruleus under Contextual Fear Conditioning.
items.authors: Shimizu M, Stavnezer AJ.

sections.text: Fear memory, a vital survival mechanism, is closely linked to posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). PTSD results in persistent negative emotional symptoms following a traumatic experience and is currently difficult to treat. Traditionally associated with the hippocampus and amygdala, recent studies have drawn attention to the locus coeruleus (LC) as an indirect modulator of arousal and stress responses. Using contextual fear conditioning and immunohistochemistry, we found that fear engrams are formed directly in the LC in the TRAP2 mouse model. Therefore, the LC appears to serve as more than an indirect modulator of fear memory, opening new strategies for treating PTSD.

items.title: Machine learning applications across living environments, activity behaviors, and mental health among older adults: a systematic review.
items.authors: Wang Y, Lan J.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Machine learning is increasingly used to examine how living environments, activity behaviors, and mental health are interconnected in later life. However, evidence across these domains remains dispersed, and the contribution of machine learning to understanding their relationships has not been systematically synthesized.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Following PRISMA 2020-informed procedures, we systematically reviewed empirical studies published between 1 January 2016 and 30 August 2026. Eligible studies included participants aged 60 years or older or reported separately extractable findings for this age group, examined relationships involving at least two of living environment, activity behaviors, and mental health, and used machine learning as a substantive component of the empirical analysis.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Of 4,337 records identified, 27 studies met the eligibility criteria. Evidence was concentrated on individual relationships between living environment, activity behaviors, and mental health, while relatively few studies considered all three domains together. Across this literature, machine learning was used to construct environmental and behavioral measures, predict behavioral and mental-health outcomes, and characterize nonlinear relationships, thresholds, interactions, and population or spatial heterogeneity. items.title: Long-acting injectable antipsychotics linked to reduced short-term disruptive life event and death.
items.authors: Han B, Butler R, Coleman KJ, Rossom RC, Li X, Waters HC, Nau CL.

sections.text: Long-acting injectable antipsychotics (LAI) may be beneficial for patients with schizophrenia (SCZ) or bipolar I disorder (BPI) compared with oral antipsychotics. We aimed to assess the association of LAI use on all-cause mortality and disruptive life events (DLE) among patients recently diagnosed with SCZ or BPI. We conducted a retrospective cohort study using adult patients meeting study eligibility criteria in Kaiser Permanente Southern California (KPSC) during 2007-2019. The index event for cohort entry was the first mental health related emergency department or inpatient encounter after initial diagnosis of SCZ or BPI. Two study arms were defined by the medication history within 180 days after index events: received LAI (LAI arm) and received oral antipsychotics only (oral-only arm). Unadjusted and adjusted two-sample comparisons were performed, where adjusted analyses used propensity score matching to balance observed characteristics. Outcomes were occurrence of specific DLEs (arrests, bankruptcy, and judgment filings), occurrence of any DLE, and all-cause mortality during the year after index events. The cohort had 3,667 patients in the oral-only arm and 218 in the LAI arm. Compared with the oral-only arm, the LAI arm had lower risks in all outcomes qualitatively. The rarity of the outcome and limited sample size in the LAI arm limited statistical power: adjusted risk difference was -1.68% for occurrences of any DLE (95% CI: -3.44%, 0.08%, p < 0.10), and -0.46% for all-cause mortality (95% CI: -0.98%, 0.06%, p < 0.10). Patients with SCZ or BPI taking LAIs may be associated with lower risk of DLE and mortality within the one-year period after index than those who took oral antipsychotics only. Larger studies are needed to further confirm these associations.

items.title: A tailored online mindfulness intervention for junior doctors: a mixed-methods study.
items.authors: Moore S, Ngo H, Auret K, Toffoli A, O'Sullivan L, Cuesta-Briand B, Hassed C, Chambers R, Mavaddat N.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Junior doctor training is stressful and associated with significant challenges, including poor mental health and burnout. Mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) are increasingly being offered within junior doctor education programs to support junior doctor wellbeing, with online platforms for delivery attracting interest.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This mixed-method randomised waitlist control trial was conducted with junior doctors across two hospitals in Western Australia. The intervention was an 8-week online mindfulness training program, with usual training as control. Outcome measures were changes from baseline to program completion (eight weeks) and then one-month follow-up for self-reported surveys of trait mindfulness, perceived stress, self-compassion, occupational stress, and work engagement. Intervention and control participants completed surveys at all three time points. Semi-structured interviews and focus groups were conducted with participants at program completion.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Seventy-two (35 intervention, 37 control) junior doctors were randomised. Seventeen did not complete the baseline measures. Data for the remaining 55 participants (28 Intervention, 27 Control) were retained for analysis. Most intervention participants formally practiced mindfulness two to three times per week for five to seven minutes however quality of formal and informal practice was low. For the intervention group, perceived stress increased at program completion (-1.4, 95% CI - 2.6, -0.3, p = 0.0151) while work engagement was decreased (-2.9, CI - 5.6, -0.2, p = 0.0355) at final follow-up. There were no significant changes in any of the outcomes for the control group at any follow-up point. Thirteen intervention participants undertook focus groups or individual interviews about their experience. Despite lack of positive quantitative findings, benefits reported regarding the program during interview included: improved self-awareness, emotion regulation, self-compassion and work productivity, as well as professional and personal relationships. Barriers to participation in the program included limited time, work stress, and challenges with elements of the intervention.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: This novel online mindfulness training program was not associated with improvements in measured outcomes including trait-mindfulness, perceived stress, self-compassion, occupational stress or work engagement for participating junior doctors. This contrasts with our qualitative findings suggesting that junior doctors experience some wellbeing benefits from participating, and with the results of our similar trial in medical students. While the dose of mindfulness practice was the same for both trials, junior doctors' adherence to practice was lower than medical students' adherence. Organisational factors such as stressful workplaces and time limitations likely minimised the impact of the mindfulness intervention in this group.

items.title: Caught between financial and psychological distress: a call for integrated financial readiness and community-based mental health interventions in the U.S.
items.authors: Ryder SN, Kovacs R, Zhang X, Marciniak T, Brown AD.

sections.text: Financial stress and mental health disorders impact much of the general population globally. In addition, studies show that mental health concerns and financial stress are highly interconnected. On the one hand, mental health concerns and substance use disorders have been linked to factors associated with financial hardship, such as debt and insecurity. On the other, financial stress has been linked to the onset and maintenance of mental health disorders. Given the gaps in access to services that address mental health disorders and financial hardship, community-based models have been developed to provide relevant services. To date, however, community-based models supporting mental health and financial stress address these issues separately, with few strategies taking an integrative approach. The adaptation of community-based models for mental health and financial readiness represents an important strategy for developing new interventions to understand the dynamics between mental health concerns and financial stress. We propose the need for research and implementation efforts directed at integrating community-based financial and mental health interventions.

items.title: Profiles of Beliefs About Adversity and Mental Health Networks in Medical Freshmen: An Ising Model and Simulation Study.
items.authors: Hu W, Luo S, Ye B, Qiu Z.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Medical freshmen face substantial psychological challenges, yet protective beliefs about adversity remain poorly characterized. Prior variable-centered research assumes homogeneity in beliefs about adversity. This research employed a person-centered, network-analytic method to uncover hidden belief profiles and assess their varied reactions to simulated interventions through the NodeIdentifyR algorithm (NIRA).

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A cross-sectional sample of 1,235 freshmen from two medical colleges in Jiangxi completed the Beliefs about Adversity Scale and the SCL-90. Latent profile analysis (LPA) identified distinct belief profiles. Ising network models were estimated for each profile, and NIRA simulations were performed to evaluate the effects of node-level alleviation and aggravation interventions on overall network activation.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The LPA revealed four distinct profiles: Low-Belief (5.0%), High-Belief (45.0%), Average-Belief (37.0%), and a novel Diligent-but-Doubtful profile (13.0%), characterized by high endorsement of effort and low expectations for positive outcomes, tentatively suggesting intra-belief conflict rather than merely low positivity. Symptom network structures showed distinct configurations across profiles: psychoticism (Low-Belief), hostility (High-Belief), anxiety (Diligent-but-Doubtful), and interpersonal sensitivity (Average-Belief) emerged as the most central nodes. A counterintuitive pattern emerged: obsessive-compulsive (OC) symptoms were a universal alleviation target across all profiles, whereas aggravation targets were profile-specific (eg, psychoticism for Low-Belief, depression for Average-Belief).

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Beliefs about adversity are not unidimensional but comprise heterogeneous, structurally distinct configurations. Given the cross-sectional design, the Diligent-but-Doubtful profile suggests that intra-belief conflict, rather than belief valence alone, may be associated with cognitive vulnerability; however, this interpretation requires replication. The divergence between universal alleviation targets and profile-specific aggravation nodes offers a heuristic for developing precision-matched mental health interventions in medical education, pending empirical validation through controlled intervention studies.

items.title: Self-perceived mental health related to coping strategies among studentsat a private university in Colombia.
items.authors: Campo-Torregroza EL, Padilla-Constante KN, Castro-Melo GP.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: According to the Colombian Association of Universities (ASCUN), 40% of university students in Colombia experience symptoms of anxiety and depression, reflecting mental health disorders.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: To identify the relationship between self-perceived mental health and coping strategies among university students.

sections.heading: Materials and methods
sections.text: This quantitative, cross-sectional, correlational study included a population of 4,107 students. A proportionate stratified random sampling approach was used to select 352 students from nine undergraduate programs at a private university in Colombia. The 12-item General Health Questionnaire (GHQ-12), supplemented with items assessing sociodemographic characteristics, and the Fernández-Abascal Coping Styles and Stress Coping Strategies Scale were used. Statistical analysis and data processing were performed using Stata 16.0.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Self-perceived mental health problems were more prevalent among female students, and the related coping strategies were: (1) problem solving, (2) seeking social support, (3) waiting, (5) emotional avoidance, (6) aggressive reaction, (9) positive reappraisal, (10) expression of coping difficulty, (11) denial, and (12) autonomy.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: In contrast to previous studies reporting a higher prevalence of students with mental health problems, the prevalence observed in the present study was lower.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: The coping strategies used by university students may determine their self-perceived mental health problems.

items.title: Psychological distress among acute coronary syndrome patients - a descriptive cross-sectional study in patients managed at an interventional cardiology unit in Sri Lanka.
items.authors: Fernando T, Navinan MR, Guruge SIT, Mendis SAE.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Mental health issues are a globally prevalent problem. Psychological distress (PD) is an emotional and behavioural response to a stressor and can even lead to mental health disease. It is also associated with cardiovascular disease including acute coronary syndrome.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A cross-sectional study was conducted to assess psychological distress using a Kessler's psychological distress scale (K10) in patients presenting with acute coronary syndrome in a primary percutaneous coronary intervention centre in Sri Lanka. Hundred and fifty-seven patients were enrolled. Data was collected from an interviewer-and self-administered questionnaires. Patient demographics, socio-economic, behavioural and clinical & therapeutic details were obtained and analysed using Chi-square tests and Polytomous Universal Model (PLUM) ordinal regression for cross comparison with varying levels of psychological distress [no distress, mild distress, moderate distress or severe distress].

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The mean age was 52.9 ± 11.01 years and 40.8% of the sampled patients had varying levels of psychological distress. On initial bivariate analysis screening recent emotional distress, inadequate sleep, regular religious activity showed statistically significant correlation with PD (P < 0.05). However, when adjusting for confounders in the multivariate PLUM ordinal regression only recent emotional disturbance (P < 0.001) [aOR = 19.71, 95% CI:8.00-48.52) and inadequate sleep duration (P = 0.019) [aOR = 2.56, 95% CI: 1.17-5.62] retained independent significance as predictors of distress severity. Other behavioural and clinical disease attributes became attenuated in the multivariate model.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Psychological distress is prevalent among patients with acute coronary syndrome. The immediate emotional burden after ACS is independently associated with patients' pre-existing emotional baseline and lifestyle biology rather than clinical disease and its severity.

items.title: Co-designed development of a vocational education and training program for peer health and social care navigators in Australia.
items.authors: Jessup RL, Said S, Cvetanovska N, Laughlin J, Pryor K, Hoak F, Mehmet H, Whicker S.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Peer health navigators (lay patient navigators) are increasingly used to support consumers to access and navigate health and social care systems, particularly for populations experiencing barriers to care. Despite growing evidence of their effectiveness, Australia lacks a nationally recognised education and training pathway to support consistent capability development for this emerging health workforce. This study describes the co-design and development of Australia's first contextualised vocational education and training program for peer health navigators.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A multi-stage, mixed-methods approach integrated evidence from a systematic review of international peer health navigator education and/or training programs, stakeholder interviews, focus groups, co-design workshops with culturally and linguistically diverse communities and curriculum co-development with subject matter experts. Findings informed the development of a capability framework for peer health navigators as well as the selection and contextualisation of units within a Certificate III in Community Services qualification specific for the education and training of peer health navigators.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The resulting curriculum comprised 12 units (33 modules) aligned with vocational education requirements and the identified capabilities and competencies required for the training of vocationally recognised practice of health navigators. Core units focused on communication, working with diverse individuals, safe work practice, and maintaining professional continuity, while elective units addressed knowledge and skills development for consumer empowerment and advocacy, addressing cultural safety, working with mental health and crisis situations, and appropriate engagement with health services and specific consumer needs such as chronic disease support. All units underwent expert review to ensure relevance, cultural responsiveness, safety, and feasibility.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: This work establishes a structured, nationally recognised education and training pathway to support the integration of peer health navigators across health and community service settings in Australia. The curriculum provides a foundation for workforce development in this emerging area of practice. Future research should evaluate implementation, learner outcomes and the impact of vocationally trained peer health navigators on service access, consumer experience and health equity.

items.title: "Something is not right": caregivers' and educators' perceptions of developmental concerns in toddlers at elevated likelihood of autism.
items.authors: Ferreira F, Bártolo A, Conde A.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: The pre-diagnostic period before an autism diagnosis is a critical yet underexplored phase for families and educators. This study aimed to explore how family caregivers and educators experience the pre-diagnostic period of toddlers at elevated likelihood of autism, focusing on perceived developmental concerns, family impact, help-seeking trajectories, and support needs.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: An exploratory qualitative design was used, based on semi-structured interviews with 15 participants (family caregivers and educators) associated with five children who screened positive for autism risk on the M-CHAT-R/F at 30 months. Data were analysed using thematic analysis.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Findings were organised into four key themes aligned with the study objectives: (1) perceived developmental challenges and their impact on family dynamics; (2) caregivers' experiences in accessing formal and informal support during the pre-diagnostic period; (3) barriers and facilitators in accessing specialised support; and (4) support needs during the pre-diagnostic period. The pre-diagnostic period was characterised by the progressive emergence of developmental concerns, particularly in communication, social interaction, emotional regulation, routines, autonomy, and sensory processing. These experiences were associated with significant impacts on family functioning, including increased caregiving demands, emotional strain, and concerns regarding the child's future. Two distinct help-seeking trajectories were identified: one marked by early recognition and proactive mobilisation of support, and another characterised by delayed help-seeking, often associated with the normalisation or minimisation of concerns. Access to support was shaped by both facilitating factors (e.g., parental sensitivity and educator involvement) and barriers (e.g., long waiting times, financial burden, and limited recognition of concerns by professionals). Caregivers also reported unmet needs, including greater access to therapeutic services, diagnostic clarification, psychoeducation, and psychological support.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Overall, the findings highlight the pre-diagnostic period as a critical and under-recognised phase of family adjustment, characterised by uncertainty and active meaning-making. abstract.text:
The pre-diagnostic period before an autism diagnosis is a critical yet underexplored phase for families and educators. This study aimed to explore how family caregivers and educators experience the pre-diagnostic period of toddlers at elevated likelihood of autism, focusing on perceived developmental concerns, family impact, help-seeking trajectories, and support needs.

An exploratory qualitative design was used, based on semi-structured interviews with 15 participants (family caregivers and educators) associated with five children who screened positive for autism risk on the M-CHAT-R/F at 30 months. Data were analysed using thematic analysis.

Findings were organised into four key themes aligned with the study objectives: (1) perceived developmental challenges and their impact on family dynamics; (2) caregivers' experiences in accessing formal and informal support during the pre-diagnostic period; (3) barriers and facilitators in accessing specialised support; and (4) support needs during the pre-diagnostic period. The pre-diagnostic period was characterised by the progressive emergence of developmental concerns, particularly in communication, social interaction, emotional regulation, routines, autonomy, and sensory processing. These experiences were associated with significant impacts on family functioning, including increased caregiving demands, emotional strain, and concerns regarding the child's future. Two distinct help-seeking trajectories were identified: one marked by early recognition and proactive mobilisation of support, and another characterised by delayed help-seeking, often associated with the normalisation or minimisation of concerns. Access to support was shaped by both facilitating factors (e.g., parental sensitivity and educator involvement) and barriers (e.g., long waiting times, financial burden, and limited recognition of concerns by professionals). Caregivers also reported unmet needs, including greater access to therapeutic services, diagnostic clarification, psychoeducation, and psychological support.

Overall, the findings highlight the pre-diagnostic period as a critical and under-recognised phase of family adjustment, characterised by uncertainty and active meaning-making. These results underscore the need for earlier validation of caregiver concerns, enhanced professional training, and more accessible, needs-based support prior to formal diagnosis.

items.title: The general mental health conditions and related factors of the occupational health physicians working in Ankara Province.
items.authors: Baki SD, Piyal B.

sections.heading: Aim
sections.text: This study aimed to evaluate the personal and occupational factors associated with the general mental health status of occupational physicians.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: In this cross-sectional survey, data were collected through a self-administered online survey consisting of the General Health Questionnaire-12 (GHQ-12) and a demographic questionnaire for occupational physicians, including items on working conditions and workplace environment.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: A total of 185 occupational physicians participated in the survey, and 44.9% of the respondents were identified as being at risk for poor mental health based on their GHQ-12 scores. To identify factors associated with GHQ-12 risk status, a multivariable logistic regression model was constructed using variables that were statistically significant in univariable analyses, as well as variables that have been shown in the literature to be related to general mental health and were considered important in terms of the conceptual framework of the study. The odds of being in the GHQ-12 at-risk group decreased as the length of service as an occupational physician increased (OR = 0.928; 95% CI: 0.875-0.985; p = 0.013). Participants exposed to any form of workplace violence or bullying had 3.238 times higher odds of being in the GHQ-12 at-risk group than those who were not exposed (OR = 3.238; 95% CI: 1.624-6.455; p < 0.001). Similarly, participants who were required to work outside regular working hours had 2.401 times higher odds of being in the GHQ-12 at-risk group than those who were not (OR = 2.401; 95% CI: 1.210-4.762; p = 0.012).

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: These findings highlight the necessity of regularly assessing the psychological well-being of occupational physicians, who play a critical role in delivering preventive health services to workers.

items.title: Reflective seminars for the promotion of mental health in medical education: a qualitative model in a Latin American context.
items.authors: Sampieri-Cabrera R, Guizar-Sánchez DP, Robles-Cabrera A, Vives-Varela T, Contla-Cervantes F.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Medical training sustains a persistent tension between academic demands, emotional well-being, and professional identity. In Latin America, mental health promotion remains scarcely integrated into the formal curriculum. This study examined a reflective seminar consisting of a single standardised four-hour session delivered once to each of 54 groups of second-year students (20 students per group; 1,080 students in total) during the preclinical phase of medical training. The study explored participants' perceptions of the seminar's pedagogical dynamics and its perceived effects.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Qualitative interpretive research was conducted using a hermeneutic-phenomenological design. Four focus groups were held with 26 research participants (14 students and 12 teachers) who had taken part in the seminar and provided written informed consent. Inductive-deductive thematic analysis combined open and axial coding, source triangulation, and collegial calibration to support interpretive rigour.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Three interrelated dimensions were identified. Perceived institutional care legitimised well-being as an academic concern. Psychological safety favoured openness, peer support, and reflective deliberation. Teachers acted as emotional facilitators and models of professional vulnerability, which participants associated with a reconfiguration of pedagogical relationships and of the hidden curriculum. Neither psychological safety nor perceived benefit was uniform: some students remained disengaged, participation was lower in one group with a more reserved facilitator, and one teacher described feeling overwhelmed when students later sought individual support.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: The reflective seminar may function as a relational pedagogical infrastructure that articulates well-being and professional identity. Participants described curricular integration, a climate of trust, and teacher modelling as enabling ecological readings of distress and as displacing individualising narratives. These findings provide qualitative evidence of plausible, perceived mechanisms by which formative interventions can humanise medical education, and they generate hypotheses for comparable contexts rather than demonstrated effects.

items.title: Tracing the impact of maternal communication deviance on joint engagement: The mediating role of maternal supportive behaviors.
items.authors: Sousa P, Hartley R, Sellwood W, Grace N, Sharp H, Hill J, Bentall RP.

sections.text: Communication Deviance is a disorganized communicative style that can disrupt shared meaning-making in parent-child interactions and is considered a risk factor for later mental health difficulties. This longitudinal study, conducted in the UK, examined whether maternal Communication Deviance assessed during pregnancy predicted joint engagement and related processes. Participants were 229 mothers (95.9% White British; M = 27.6 years, SD = 6.1). Maternal Communication Deviance was assessed antenatally, and mother-child dyads were observed during play at 30-months. Communication Deviance predicted lower total joint engagement, including supported (β = -.18, p = .007), coordinated (β = -.17, p = .016), and symbol-infused joint engagement (β = -.24, p < .001), and was associated with reduced supportive behaviors (β = -.40, p < .001) and dyadic attunement (β = -.31, p < .001). Mediation analyses indicated that supportive behaviors accounted for the associations between Communication Deviance and joint engagement outcomes. These findings suggest that Communication Deviance may constrain children's opportunities for shared attention and meaning making. The study supports developmental models that highlight early communicative processes as foundational to socio-cognitive and relational development and identifies supportive behaviors as a potential target for interventions promoting early mental health and parent-child interaction. KEY FINDINGS: Higher maternal Communication Deviance during pregnancy predicted less Total, Supported, Coordinated, and Symbol-infused joint engagement at 30 months. Reduced maternal supportive behaviors fully explained the link between Communication Deviance and lower joint engagement and dyadic attunement. Maternal Communication Deviance may act as an early environmental risk factor, highlighting the importance of supporting maternal responsiveness to promote healthy development. STATEMENT OF RELEVANCE: This study examines how maternal Communication Deviance measured during pregnancy predicts joint engagement and dyadic attunement at 30 months, processes central to early socio-cognitive and relational development. By identifying maternal supportive behaviors as a key mechanism linking Communication Deviance to interactional quality, the research highlights a modifiable target for early intervention. Findings advance understanding of early environmental risk factors and inform strategies to support parent-child interactions, directly addressing foundational processes relevant to child and early childhood mental health.

items.title: Diagnostic challenges of atypical neuroleptic malignant syndrome after laparoscopic surgery for perforated peritonitis in a patient with class II obesity: a case report.
items.authors: Sakata K, Hamada J, Watanabe A, Shoji W, Shibuya N, Hata T.
items.journal: International journal of surgery case reports

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Atypical neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) can be difficult to recognize in the postoperative setting because its clinical features may overlap with those of persistent infection.

sections.heading: Presentation of case
sections.text: A 53-year-old man with class II obesity (body-mass index of 35 kg/m^2) and bipolar disorder treated with multiple psychotropic medications was hospitalized for sepsis and renal failure. He developed abdominal distension, and computed tomography revealed pneumoperitoneum without an identifiable perforation site. Laparoscopic exploration identified a transverse colon perforation, which was followed by a diverting colostomy with lavage and drainage. Although septic shock improved postoperatively, persistent fever and leukocytosis (>30 000/µL) persisted. He developed diaphoresis, sialorrhea, dysphagia, dysarthria, and altered consciousness. Repeated investigations identified no infectious source. A hematologic disorder was suspected but subsequently excluded. Based on the clinical course, atypical neuroleptic malignant syndrome associated with perioperative discontinuation of antipsychotic medications was considered the most likely diagnosis. Resumption of psychotropic medications was followed by gradual clinical improvement.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: Persistent postoperative fever initially suggested uncontrolled infection, whereas subsequent clinical and laboratory findings raised suspicion of a hematological disorder. In retrospect, persistent autonomic and extrapyramidal symptoms, together with persistent fever despite improving sepsis, were important clues to atypical NMS.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: This case highlights the diagnostic challenges of atypical postoperative NMS and supports laparoscopic exploration for peritonitis of unknown origin. Postoperative NMS should be considered in patients recently withdrawn from psychotropic medications when persistent fever and leukocytosis are accompanied by autonomic and extrapyramidal symptoms that are not fully explained by infection.

items.title: Prenatal SARS-CoV-2 infection, COVID-19 vaccination, and preschool neurodevelopment: A confounder-adjusted cohort study.
items.authors: Rizzo M, Tubassum R, Milazzo F, Schmitt Y, Lieb W, Perez-Rodriguez MLM, de Witte LD, Bergink V, Rommel AS.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: The impact of maternal SARS-CoV-2 infection and COVID-19 vaccination during pregnancy on child neurodevelopment remains unclear, with most studies limited by small samples and short follow-up periods. This prospective cohort study assesses internalizing, externalizing, total problem behaviors, and social responsiveness in children prenatally exposed or unexposed to maternal SARS-CoV-2 infection or COVID-19 vaccination.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: The study leveraged a large NYC pregnancy cohort with detailed information on maternal infection and vaccination during pregnancy. Outcomes included parent-reported CBCL and SRS. Analyses were adjusted for key sociodemographic and clinical factors, including race/ethnicity, maternal mental health condition, and child age at assessment.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The study included 675 children (mean age = 3.2 years, SD = 0.8, 50.7% male), comprising 118 children prenatally exposed to SARS-CoV-2 and 557 unexposed. Regression analyses showed no significant associations between prenatal SARS-CoV-2 exposure and CBCL Internalizing ( β  = 0.04 [95% CI: -0.85, 0.88]), CBCL Externalizing ( β  = -0.31 [95% CI: -1.41, 0.87]), CBCL Total Problems ( β  = -0.50 [95% CI: -3.46, 2.51]), and SRS ( β  = -0.60 [95% CI: -4.09, 3.17]) scores. Comparing children prenatally exposed ( n  = 68) and unexposed ( n  = 607) to COVID-19 vaccination revealed no significant associations with CBCL Internalizing ( β  = 0.41 [95% CI: -0.52, 1.44]), CBCL Externalizing ( β  = 1.42 [95% CI: -0.32, 2.95]), CBCL Total Problems ( β  = 2.13 [95% CI: -1.22, 6.15]), and SRS ( β  = -3.65 [95% CI: -7.93, 0.32]) scores. Sociodemographic covariates, such as race/ethnicity and educational attainment, were significantly associated with all neurodevelopmental outcomes.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Prenatal exposure to SARS-CoV-2 infection or COVID-19 vaccination was not associated with adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes in preschool children. Sociodemographic factors showed stronger associations than infection or vaccination, underscoring the importance of confounder adjustment. Findings provide reassurance to pregnant individuals regarding potential long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes in offspring following SARS-CoV-2 infection or COVID-19 vaccination during pregnancy.

items.title: Promotion of sensorimotor and attentional development for infants at elevated likelihood of autism: single case experimental design of novel caregiver implemented NDBI.
items.authors: Simacek JJ, Worthley E, Dimian A, Gunderson J, Beavis H, Chubb L, Tran P, Meyer P, Wolff JJ.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Infants with familial autism are at elevated likelihood for future neurodevelopmental needs, including autism spectrum disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, and clinically significant cognitive and behavioral challenges. Science is advancing the near-future ability to determine presymptomatic and prodromal periods of neurodevelopmental disabilities in infancy. To meet the needs of these infants and their families, proactive intervention and support models must advance in tandem.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: The present study investigated a novel, telehealth-based approach to caregiver coaching within a naturalistic and developmental behavioral intervention framework to address behavioral priors of attention and sensorimotor responding with nine infants at elevated likelihood of autism due to family history. We sought to answer a primary research question on the functional relation of the NDBI intervention on proximal infant behaviors related to sensorimotor and attentional responding during three, concurrent multiple baseline designs across infant/caregiver dyads. Secondary questions on the feasibility of the study and pre/post characterization of distal measures of infant development were also included.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Based on descriptive analysis of attendance data and visual analysis of SCED data, there was promising feasibility and initial single case experimental design evidence on the idiographic efficacy particularly on motor imitation, although results were variable across participants and targeted responses. Following iterations on the study design, the final procedures in the third multiple baseline design led to the most consistent changes across dyads.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Given the known importance on earlier identification of autism spectrum disorder/neurodevelopmental disabilities (ASD/NDD) coupled with the nascent stage of intervention research at prodromal or presymptomatic periods, intervention research needs to develop in lockstep with earlier identification. Flexibility appears to be an important component of the present intervention and other emerging models of infant intervention for families with young children and with multiple children with or at elevated likelihood of ASD/NDD.

sections.heading: Trial registration
sections.text: This study was retrospectively registered at OSF. https://osf.io/6tuyx/overview?view_only=2c85f33fd60b496f86ecb09625e6e4b7, Clinical Trial Registration: not applicable.

items.title: Effects of infertility on relationship quality and mental health outcomes in sub-Saharan Africa: A scoping review.
items.authors: Juma K, Kairu C, Nungo MA, Chepkoech M, Olwanda E, Odunga SA, Ouedraogo R, Ushie BA, Wado YD.

sections.text: Infertility is associated with significant psychosocial challenges, and relationship strain yet remains underprioritized in sub-Saharan African policy and research. We conducted a scoping review to examine the effects of infertility on relationship quality and mental health outcomes among people experiencing infertility in sub-Saharan Africa. We utilized the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology for scoping reviews and reported following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews. We searched databases including PubMed/MEDLINE, CINAHL, Web of Science, JSTOR, Scopus, Academic Search Complete, PsycINFO, and the Psychology and Behavioral Science Collection. Eligible articles focused on the effects of infertility on mental health and relationship quality in women, men, and couples experiencing infertility and were published between January 2000 and November 2025. We extracted data and conducted an iterative narrative synthesis. We included 70 articles: 36 quantitative, 5 mixed methods, and 29 qualitative. Four key themes emerged, which fit within the socio-ecological model: 1) infertility and relationship quality, 2) infertility and mental health, stigma and discrimination, 3) adaptive coping mechanisms, and 4) maladaptive coping mechanisms. Infertility was associated with anxiety, depression, and emotional distress. Studies revealed profound experiences of isolation and grief over unfulfilled reproductive goals, compounded by societal pressures. Diminished relationship quality was a common outcome among individuals with infertility, manifesting as intimate partner violence, verbal and emotional abuse, loss of intimacy, infidelity, and separation or divorce. Couples with infertility attempted multiple care pathways, including religious, biomedical, and traditional care. Lack of psychosocial support was common, and individuals often coped through substance and drug abuse, isolation, and active avoidance. Complexity of the relationship between infertility, mental health, and relationship quality, reinforces the need for urgent integrated individual and structural interventions that promote holistic fertility care and social support.

items.title: Antiseizure Medication Dispensing Before and After Initiation of Antidementia Medicines: A Population-Based Matched Cohort Study.
items.authors: Almeida OP, Etherton-Beer C, Sanfilippo FM, Preen DB, Page A.

sections.heading: Purpose
sections.text: Seizures and behavioural and psychiatric features may prompt antiseizure medication (ASM) use in dementia. We examined whether increased ASM dispensing precedes or follows initiation of antidementia treatment to inform hypotheses about when these indications emerge.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Using the Australian Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) 10% sample, we matched people aged ≥ 50 years with incident antidementia dispensing in 2018-2021 1:1 to controls without antidementia dispensing (2013-2024) by age, sex, index year and diabetes and hypertension treatment. We compared annual ASM dispensing (ATC N03, excluding gabapentinoids) from 5 years before to 3 years after initiation using McNemar's test and interrupted time series analysis. Sensitivity analyses re-matched on Rx-Risk comorbidity and removed the survival requirement.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Among 4385 matched pairs (59.8% women; mean age 78.3 years), ASM dispensing was higher in cases 5 years before initiation (2.7% vs. 1.8%; ratio 1.53, 95% CI = 1.15-2.03) and the difference widened after initiation (year 3: 9.1% vs. 2.4%; ratio 3.85, 95% CI = 3.13-4.75). Valproate accounted for most of the excess (year 3 ratio 6.97, 95% CI = 4.80-10.12). Levetiracetam dispensing rose gradually from year -3 and was higher after initiation (year 3 ratio 2.30, 95% CI = 1.51-3.50). Matching on comorbidity attenuated pre-initiation differences (year -5 ratio 1.42). The excess was greater at ages 50-79 years.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: ASM dispensing, most noticeably valproate, was higher in people with antidementia medicine dispensing than in controls, modestly before and markedly after initiation. Behavioural and psychiatric indications seem to predominate, with a smaller seizure-related contribution possibly beginning before treatment, although dispensing data cannot confirm indications. Valproate use warrants review.

items.title: What knowledge, skills, and attributes are sought by employers hiring occupational therapists to work in mental health services?
items.authors: Aguey-Zinsou M, Yule E, Illingworth B, Milliken Y.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Occupational therapy education programs need to prepare graduates for contemporary mental health practice. Previous research has identified knowledge, skills, and attributes prioritised by clinicians, educators, and consumers, but contemporary Australian employer perspectives are less well understood. This study explored the knowledge, skills, and attributes sought by employers hiring occupational therapists to work in mental health services in New South Wales, Australia.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A qualitatively driven mixed methods design was used across four sequential phases. Phases 1 and 4 involved qualitative content analysis of job advertisements for mental health roles in New South Wales that were open to occupational therapists. Phase 2 involved an online survey of employers about their hiring priorities, and Phase 3 involved a follow-up focus group to further explore survey findings.

sections.heading: Consumer and community involvement
sections.text: Consumer and employer advisory panels informed survey development, supported interpretation of emerging findings and advised on dissemination.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Across the four phases, 37 key areas of knowledge, skills, and attributes were identified. Employer priorities included knowledge of mental health conditions, recovery-oriented practice, trauma-informed care, assessment, communication, therapeutic relationship-building, collaboration, reflective practice, and self-care. Employers also identified future-facing capabilities, including knowledge of the National Disability Insurance Scheme, ability to use telehealth, and commitment to environmentally sustainable practice. Job advertisements showed that generic mental health roles remained common across both time points, and Phase 4 advertisements included a greater proportion of regional roles.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Employer perspectives aligned with recovery-oriented, trauma-informed, and person-centred practice, while also highlighting employability, relational attributes, and emerging service-system capabilities. Findings can inform mental health occupational therapy curriculum by supporting integration of knowledge, skills, and attributes across authentic practice contexts and by helping graduates articulate the occupational therapy contribution in generic and interdisciplinary mental health roles.
