items.title: Disease-specific cognitive impacts in aging: a large-scale longitudinal analysis of chronic conditions and demographic modifiers.
items.authors: Wang S, Song F, Xiang B, Deng L.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Cognitive decline represents a major public health concern among aging populations, yet the domain-specific impacts of chronic diseases remain poorly understood. This study examined associations between chronic diseases and specific cognitive domains, exploring heterogeneity across population subgroups.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: We analyzed longitudinal data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study across three waves (2015, 2018, 2020; ~2-3-year intervals), comprising 16,027 participants aged 45-90 years (35,247 observations). Continuous cognitive outcomes (orientation, memory, computation, and total score) were standardized (z-scores), so β represents the SD-unit difference in cognitive score for disease presence versus absence; drawing ability, a binary outcome, was analyzed via logistic regression and reported as an odds ratio. These outcomes were modeled against 14 chronic conditions using mixed-effects models adjusted for demographic, lifestyle, and health covariates and for co-occurring conditions. P-values were corrected for multiple comparisons (56 tests), and effect modification by education and sex was tested formally.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Nine of fourteen conditions remained significant after correction. Memory-related disease showed the broadest impairment, affecting total cognition (β=-0.292, P < 0.001), orientation (β=-0.326), and memory (β=-0.190). Chronic lung disease (β=-0.062) and emotional/psychiatric disorders (β=-0.158) were also negatively associated with cognition, as was stroke (β=-0.127). Heart disease (β=+0.109) and liver disease (β=+0.087) showed unexpected positive associations, which we interpret cautiously given the absence of clinical severity data. Education significantly modified the associations for stroke, chronic lung disease, and emotional/psychiatric disorders (all P < 0.05), with greater vulnerability among more-educated participants; no disease-by-sex interaction was significant.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Chronic diseases show distinct, domain-specific cognitive impacts, with education-but not sex-modifying a subset of these associations. These findings support disease-specific rather than uniform approaches to cognitive risk assessment in aging populations.

items.title: Evidence generation for diabetes prevention and treatment through the integration of clinical medicine, nutritional epidemiology, and behavioral science.
items.authors: Baden MY.

sections.text: Diet and other lifestyle factors are central to diabetes prevention and management. Effective dietary and lifestyle support requires consideration of differences in pathophysiology, food culture, and living circumstances. This narrative review summarizes our research integrating clinical medicine, nutritional epidemiology, and behavioral science, with a particular focus on diet quality. Analyses of large US cohorts showed that higher-quality plant-based diets were associated with lower risks of stroke and mortality. In longitudinal biomarker analyses, increases in healthful plant-based diet scores were associated with favorable changes in high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, whereas increases in unhealthful plant-based diet scores were associated with unfavorable changes in inflammatory biomarkers. Metabolite profiles related to healthful plant-based diets were also associated with lower type 2 diabetes risk. Building on earlier work on adiponectin and type 1 diabetes, our studies in Japan showed that even small weight changes were associated with type 2 diabetes risk, depending on age and baseline body mass index. Visceral fat correlated with ectopic fat, and fast eating and eating late at night were associated with greater pancreatic fat deposition. In older adults, lower sweet taste sensitivity was associated with frailty and poorer mental health-related quality of life. These findings suggest that diet quality and lifestyle should be assessed together with each person's metabolic characteristics and living circumstances. Intervention and implementation studies based on this largely observational evidence are the next step toward individualized diabetes prevention and care.

items.title: Decision-making processes underlying digital mental health intervention adoption among adolescents and young adults with common mental health issues: An integrated DEMATEL-ISM approach.
items.authors: Wang Y, Liu J, Zhu S.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: Despite their potential, digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) are underutilized among adolescents and young adults (AYAs) with common mental health issues. While prior work has synthesized facilitators and barriers to DMHI adoption, the decision-making processes across heterogeneous AYA remain insufficiently understood. This study aimed to understand DMHI adoption decisions by examining the relative importance and underlying pathways of identified factors within AYA subgroups.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Participants in this cross-sectional study were recruited from secondary schools and universities in Hong Kong. The Decision-Making Trial and Evaluation Laboratory (DEMATEL) was applied to reveal factor importance and cause-effect relationships, while the Interpretive Structural Modelling (ISM) approach was used to map hierarchical structures.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Based on 14 facilitators and 13 barriers to DMHI adoption, the DEMATEL results suggested that, for adolescents, endorsements and motivational challenges emerged as the most central factors, while the supportive environment and technical issues were the most influential. Among young adults, universality and retention issues were the most central, with content engagement and technical issues exerting the greatest influence. Notable differences were observed regarding the driving mechanisms behind adoption decisions: adolescents emphasised both intervention-specific and individual-level drivers, whereas young adults primarily focused on intervention-related concerns, including high quality and effect and design limitations.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: This exploratory study offers a systematic, user-centred perspective on DMHI adoption processes, with developmental contrasts highlighting the need for more age-sensitive guidance in intervention design and implementation. These insights may provide a preliminary basis for future research on resource allocation and policy development, with further evidence from larger and more demographically balanced samples needed to support broader policy implications.

items.title: Comparative efficacy and safety of quetiapine versus other atypical antipsychotics for behavioral and psychological symptoms in Alzheimer's disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.authors: Wang J, Chen W, Zhang Z.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: The management of behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) in Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains a significant challenge. While atypical antipsychotics are used, their comparative efficacy and safety, particularly for quetiapine, are not well-established within a homogeneous AD population. This meta-analysis aimed to directly compare the efficacy and safety of quetiapine versus other active pharmacological agents (primarily risperidone and olanzapine) for BPSD specifically in patients with AD.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, CNKI, and WanFang databases was conducted up to March 15, 2024, for randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The primary efficacy outcome was treatment failure (lack of clinical improvement). Safety outcomes included specific adverse events. Data were pooled using random-effects models to calculate odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Twenty-five RCTs involving 2143 participants were included. The pooled analysis of 16 studies (n=1384) demonstrated that quetiapine was associated with significantly lower odds of treatment failure compared to other atypical antipsychotics (OR 0.66, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.89, P = 0.006). In pre-specified subgroup analyses, quetiapine showed significant superiority over risperidone (OR 0.50, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.75, P = 0.0009) and a non-significant trend favoring quetiapine over olanzapine (OR 0.90, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.38, P = 0.62). Regarding safety, quetiapine was associated with a substantially and significantly lower risk of extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) (OR 0.17, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.33, P<0.00001). No significant differences were found for other common adverse events such as somnolence, dizziness, or constipation.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: This meta-analysis suggests that quetiapine may offer a potential efficacy advantage for alleviating BPSD in patients with AD, particularly when compared to risperidone, while demonstrating comparable overall effectiveness to other atypicals. Its most distinguishing feature is a substantially lower risk of extrapyramidal symptoms. Interpretation of these findings must be tempered by the moderate risk of bias in constituent trials, the necessary harmonization of disparate efficacy metrics, and the scarcity of long-term safety data. Quetiapine may serve as a neurologically better-tolerated option when non-pharmacological strategies are insufficient, pending careful, time-limited use.

items.title: Mental health promotion knowledge and practices of nursing students: A qualitative study.
items.authors: Legwabe RC, van Wyk NC, Bhana-Pema VM.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: High levels of mental distress have been documented among nursing students, but only a few seek help to promote or manage their mental health. Although health promotion is included in their curricula and institutional mental health services are provided to support them in managing the stress they experience during their training, it appears as if the students do not practice mental health promotion for themselves.

sections.heading: Aim
sections.text: The study aimed to explore and describe nursing students' personal knowledge and the systemic barriers to mental health promotion.

sections.heading: Setting
sections.text: The research was done at a nursing education institution in the Gauteng Province of South Africa.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: An exploratory, descriptive contextual qualitative study was conducted with eleven undergraduate students during the 2024-2025 academic year. Data were collected through individual, semi-structured face-to-face interviews until saturation was reached, followed by a thematic analysis.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Three categories were identified, namely 'rely on self, family and friends,' 'depend on lecturers and institutional support services' and 'the need for mental health promotion for students'.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Nursing students at the institution were partially knowledgeable about mental health promotion but not all practised appropriate health-promoting mechanisms when dealing with academic and personal challenges.

sections.heading: Contribution
sections.text: Nursing students need to be supported in their academic journey to become professional nurses. The authors recommend that institutions should adopt mental health-supportive campus cultures to improve students' mental health, encourage the maintenance of peer support groups and initiate extracurricular health-promoting activities.

items.title: Public Perceptions on Turning Normal Emotions and Appearance Concerns into Medical Concerns: A Cross-Sectional Study in Bangladesh.
items.authors: Yasmin F, Banna MHA, Billal M, Mita FA, Rana MS, Hossain GMS, Mia MT, Hossain MA.

sections.heading: Introduction and aim
sections.text: Medicalization is the process through which ordinary human experiences, behaviors and social concerns are redefined and managed as medical conditions. It now extends to everyday emotions such as sadness, stress and anxiety, and to appearance-related concerns. This trend can improve access to care. It also raises concerns about overdiagnosis, treatment dependency and reduced personal coping. This study explored public perceptions of emotional and appearance-related medicalization in Bangladesh. It also examined whether demographic factors, treatment exposure and perceived media pressure are associated with these perceptions.

sections.heading: Materials and methods
sections.text: A quantitative cross-sectional online survey was conducted with 397 participants aged 15 to 54 years. Participants were recruited through non-probability convenience sampling between June and September 2025. An expert-reviewed questionnaire was administered through Google Forms. Nine hypotheses were tested using a one-sample proportion test, Chi-square tests, Mann-Whitney U tests, Spearman's rank correlations, K-means clustering and binary logistic regression.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Most respondents (74.8%) agreed that normal emotions and life challenges are increasingly treated as medical problems. Awareness of medicalization was associated with education but not with gender. Education was the only significant demographic predictor of belief in over-medicalization (OR = 1.49), although the model explained little variance. Respondents with treatment exposure agreed more strongly than those without such exposure. Perceived helpfulness differed by treatment type, and medication alone received the highest share of "helpful" ratings. Belief that labeling emotions reduces natural coping was positively correlated with belief that it increases medication overuse (ρ = 0.30). Perceived media pressure was strongly correlated with the belief that appearance-related medicalization harms self-esteem (ρ = 0.51). Cluster analysis identified three attitudinal groups: Concerned, Neutral and Skeptical.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Respondents widely recognized and critically evaluated the medicalization of normal emotional and appearance-related experiences. Critical views were more common among more educated respondents and those with treatment exposure. These findings support balanced clinical practice, emotionally literate public discourse and caution in labeling normal experiences as disorders. Because a convenience sample was used, the results describe the surveyed respondents rather than the wider Bangladeshi population.

abstract.text:
Medicalization is the process through which ordinary human experiences, behaviors and social concerns are redefined and managed as medical conditions. It now extends to everyday emotions such as sadness, stress and anxiety, and to appearance-related concerns. This trend can improve access to care. It also raises concerns about overdiagnosis, treatment dependency and reduced personal coping. This study explored public perceptions of emotional and appearance-related medicalization in Bangladesh. It also examined whether demographic factors, treatment exposure and perceived media pressure are associated with these perceptions.

A quantitative cross-sectional online survey was conducted with 397 participants aged 15 to 54 years. Participants were recruited through non-probability convenience sampling between June and September 2025. An expert-reviewed questionnaire was administered through Google Forms. Nine hypotheses were tested using a one-sample proportion test, Chi-square tests, Mann-Whitney U tests, Spearman's rank correlations, K-means clustering and binary logistic regression.

Most respondents (74.8%) agreed that normal emotions and life challenges are increasingly treated as medical problems. Awareness of medicalization was associated with education but not with gender. Education was the only significant demographic predictor of belief in over-medicalization (OR = 1.49), although the model explained little variance. Respondents with treatment exposure agreed more strongly than those without such exposure. Perceived helpfulness differed by treatment type, and medication alone received the highest share of "helpful" ratings. Belief that labeling emotions reduces natural coping was positively correlated with belief that it increases medication overuse (ρ = 0.30). Perceived media pressure was strongly correlated with the belief that appearance-related medicalization harms self-esteem (ρ = 0.51). Cluster analysis identified three attitudinal groups: Concerned, Neutral and Skeptical.

Respondents widely recognized and critically evaluated the medicalization of normal emotional and appearance-related experiences. Critical views were more common among more educated respondents and those with treatment exposure. These findings support balanced clinical practice, emotionally literate public discourse and caution in labeling normal experiences as disorders. Because a convenience sample was used, the results describe the surveyed respondents rather than the wider Bangladeshi population.

Because a convenience sample was used, the results describe the surveyed respondents rather than the wider Bangladeshi population.

items.title: Spatially localized fMRI metrics as predictive and highly distinct state-independent fingerprints.
items.authors: Larabi DI, Gell M, Amico E, Eickhoff SB, Patil KR.

sections.text: Precision medicine and the investigation of brain-behavior associations require biomarkers that are stable (low intraindividual variability) and unique (high-interindividual variability) at the same time, hence calling them "fingerprints". The functional connectome (FC) has good "fingerprint properties", as individuals can be accurately identified in a database based on their FC. Importantly, research has shown lower intraindividual variability of more localized measures of brain function, such as regional homogeneity (ReHo) and (fractional) amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations ((f)ALFF), compared with the FC. Additionally, the predictiveness of behavior using the FC is modest at best. Here, with fMRI data from two publicly available datasets, we demonstrate that individuals can be identified with near-perfect accuracies using local functional fingerprints, especially the regional homogeneity (ReHo) fingerprint. Further analyses reveal that the dorsal attention network contributes most to the individual "uniqueness" of the ReHo fingerprint. Moreover, using a machine learning setup, we find that intraindividual variability of the ReHo fingerprint across sessions shows predictive signal for individual-level intelligence, albeit with model performance dependent on the condition. Last, using two other publicly available datasets, clinical applicability is demonstrated with high fingerprint accuracies and a significant correlation between fingerprint stability and intelligence in individuals with schizophrenia. Altogether, our findings suggest that the ReHo fingerprint is a good candidate for further exploration of applicability in precision medicine.

items.title: Challenges faced by the nurses working in Child and Adolescent Psychiatry - A qualitative study.
items.authors: Govindan R, Rajeswari B, Kommu JVS, Vilson AA.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Nurses working in Child and Adolescent Psychiatry (CAP) face many challenges. This article explores the experiences of nurses working in a specific area by using a qualitative research design.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Twenty-six nursing officers were purposively selected and interviewed. The study was conducted and reported in accordance with the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research checklist.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Various challenges related to parents, administration, safety, and security were identified. The participants also stated that working in CAP is entirely different from working in adult psychiatric settings, in terms of the physical setup and communication.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: The participants suggested that organising regular sensitization program, promoting higher education, and Continuing Nursing Education would be more helpful for better nursing care.

items.title: Evaluating determinants of treatment delay and access gaps in common mental disorders across rural versus urban India.
items.authors: Kaur P, Kaur T.

sections.heading: Aim
sections.text: To assess rural-urban differences in treatment delay and treatment access gap among individuals with common mental disorders and to identify factors associated with delayed care.

sections.heading: Materials and methods
sections.text: This cross-sectional study included 480 participants (242 rural, 238 urban) diagnosed with common mental disorders. Data were collected using structured tools, including Patient Health Questionnaire-9 and Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7. Treatment delay and associated factors were analyzed using descriptive statistics and multivariate logistic regression.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Rural participants had significantly longer treatment delays compared to urban participants (median 18 months vs 4 months, P < 0.001) and higher treatment access gaps. Prolonged delay was associated with higher symptom severity. Multivariate analysis identified perceived stigma, financial constraints, consultation with traditional healers, and distance to healthcare facilities as independent predictors of delayed treatment.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Significant rural-urban disparities exist in treatment delay and access to mental healthcare. Addressing stigma, improving mental health literacy, and strengthening primary healthcare services, particularly in rural areas, are essential to reduce delays and improve outcomes.

items.title: Child health challenges in the 2025 Sumatra flood and landslide: Lessons for disaster risk reduction and emergency response.
items.authors: Kadafi KT, Saputro DD, Leman MM, Aslinar A, Nasution BB, Anantyo DT, Puspaningtyas NW, Pohan FZ, Wirahmadi A, Purwana INA, Reza M, Rahman MABHA, Effendi JA, Prawira Y, Adriansyah R, Raihan R, Nurdin A, Yanuarso PB.

sections.text: In late 2025, catastrophic floods and landslides struck Sumatra, Indonesia, causing widespread destruction and nearly 1200 fatalities. Children were among the most severely affected, experiencing acute health problems, disruptions in essential healthcare services and significant psychosocial distress. This essay employs an evidence-informed analytical approach, integrating contemporaneous official reports, available scientific literature, international disaster risk reduction (DRR) frameworks, Emergency Medical Team (EMT) standards and the authors' direct field experience during the disaster response. The disaster is examined across the disaster management cycle, including prevention, mitigation, preparedness, emergency response and recovery, to identify gaps between established child-centred disaster management principles and their practical implementation. The analysis demonstrates that, despite national policies and international guidance, implementation was inconsistent. Many children experienced preventable illnesses, interruptions in chronic medical care, inadequate continuity of paediatric healthcare and unmet psychosocial needs because of coordination challenges, limited child-focused preparedness and fragmented service delivery. The findings highlight that integrating child-centred DRR principles with specialised paediatric emergency training, strengthened EMT deployment, continuity of essential child health services, coordinated mental health support and multisectoral collaboration can improve disaster preparedness and emergency response. The lessons learned provide practical guidance for strengthening child-centred DRR, improving emergency response systems and informing policy development that better integrates child protection and paediatric healthcare into all phases of disaster management.

items.title: Intentional Pencil Ingestion - A Case Report of a Sharp Ingested Foreign Body.
items.authors: Gan F, Mercado N, Gowder A, Ng D, Ghassemzadeh S, Costumbrado J.
items.journal: Journal of education & teaching in emergency medicine

sections.text: Treating foreign body ingestion in the emergency department (ED) is common; however, certain ingestions may be immediately life-threatening, depending on the object because sharp objects pose the greatest risk for gastrointestinal injury, including perforation and obstruction.1 This is a case of an adult male who arrived at the ED with suicidal ideation and reported ingesting a pencil two days prior. He presented with abdominal pain and hematochezia. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis identified the pencil in the distal ileum. The patient was admitted for surgical evaluation and monitoring. Remarkably, the pencil was passed spontaneously in the stool on hospital day six without signs of colonic perforation. This case illustrates how selected cases of high-risk foreign body ingestion may be managed conservatively, though close monitoring is critical given the risks of perforation, obstruction, or failure of progression.

sections.text: Abdominal pain, CT, foreign body ingestion, mental health.

items.title: Impaired discrimination of negative facial emotions in pure motor ALS.
items.authors: Meyer A, Semenkova A, Wezel S, Weber M, Schweikert K, Schläger R, Wendebourg J, Piguet O, Berres M, Braun N, Lulé D, Sollberger M.

sections.heading: Background and objectives
sections.text: Emotion recognition deficits in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) remain debated. We investigated whether patients with pure motor ALS (without cognitive and behavioural disturbances) and without clinically relevant mood disturbances are impaired in discriminating negative facial emotions, using a test without ceiling effects.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This cross-sectional study included 35 patients with pure motor ALS, based on the revised Strong criteria and operationalised using the Edinburgh Cognitive and Behavioural ALS Screen (ECAS), without clinically relevant mood disturbances, alongside 35 age-, sex-, and education-matched cognitively and psychiatrically healthy controls. All participants completed a shortened five-emotion version of the Facial Emotion Intensity Rating Test - Congruent and Incongruent and the Facial Sex Matching Task (FSMT), a brief screening measure of non-emotional facial discrimination.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Pure motor ALS patients showed poorer discrimination among negative facial emotions than healthy controls (p = 0.011, Cohen's d = 0.63). The group difference did not differ significantly across anger, fear, sadness, and disgust (p = 0.178). Similarly, the group difference in discrimination among negative emotions did not differ significantly from that in discrimination between negative emotions and happiness (p = 0.459). The two groups did not differ significantly on the FSMT.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Discrimination of negative facial emotions was impaired in patients with pure motor ALS, suggesting that classification based on ECAS screening may underestimate social-cognitive involvement. Our findings are compatible with the concept of an ALS-frontotemporal spectrum disorder. Whether impaired emotion discrimination relates to additional cognitive or behavioural impairment remains to be determined. The clinical utility and reliability of our measure require further study.

items.title: A Blueprint for National and International Healthcare Data Ecosystems: Learning From Building STRONG-AYA.
items.authors: Stark D, Lindner O, Hanebaum S, Hughes N, Kosir U, Van Der Graaf W, Husson O, Wee L, Members of the Strong‐AYA Consortium.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Healthcare systems aim for continuous improvement to ensure excellent clinical outcomes, including optimized quality of life. This relies on accurate data and evaluation patient-centered as well as biomedical outcomes. This data increasingly arises from real-world data (RWD). We are using this data across a multi-national European consortium, to create a Learning Healthcare System, improve care, policy, and ultimately patients' outcomes.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: STRONG-AYA is an interdisciplinary community, led from the Netherlands Cancer Institute, working across frequent consensus meetings, surveys, questionnaire design, data collection, synthesis and privacy-preserving federated analysis (in Vantage6), to ethically study and apply clinical and patient-centered outcomes data to learn about healthcare systems for Adolescents and Young Adults (AYAs) diagnosed with cancer when aged 15-39. The young people themselves are at the heart of our decision-making, and we work to make our data analyses transparent.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: A harmonized 'Core Outcome Set' was agreed with all stakeholders. We developed definitions and data science methodological approaches, aligned with Learning Healthcare System practices. We have built AYA cancer data ecosystems, at local, national and European levels, to combine informatics with lived experience, clinical and scientific interpretation, based upon initial 'use cases' of the mental health consequences and cancer survival rates. We are applying those insights in real time individual clinical care, individual patient education and support as well as service level metrics.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: The Strong-AYA Learning Healthcare System for AYA-onset cancer can empower discovery by health researchers, digital innovation, and innovative insights for patients, clinicians, managers and policymakers who aim for transformational improvements in the quality and outcomes of current clinical practice though the development of a Learning Healthcare System in AYA-onset cancer care. Sustainability is our next major challenge.

items.title: The anti-phage defense system GAPS4 is a double-edged sword that sensitizes bacteria to DNA-damaging agents.
items.authors: Mahata T, Kanarek K, Haldar A, Ragavan RM, Shur G, Yehia R, Burstein D, Haitin Y, Qimron U, Salomon D.

sections.text: The arms race between bacteria and bacteriophages (phages) gave rise to multiple layers of antagonistic mechanisms, many of which remain unexplored. Here, we investigated the widespread anti-phage defense system GAPS4. We found that GAPS4 forms a heterotetrameric complex containing active PD-(D/E)xK phosphodiesterase domains. It is triggered upon sensing DNA damage, leading to genomic DNA degradation and cell suicide. We further demonstrated that this activation mechanism renders GAPS4 a double-edged sword, sensitizing bacteria to various DNA-targeting antibacterial agents. Collectively, our findings reveal a possible evolutionary trade-off between anti-phage defense and immunity against interbacterial antagonism.

items.title: Aphasic status epilepticus presenting with prominent psychiatric symptoms: A case report.
items.authors: Yamada Y, Takahashi S, Fujiwara M.
items.journal: PCN reports : psychiatry and clinical neurosciences

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Aphasic status epilepticus (ASE) is a subtype of nonconvulsive status epilepticus characterized by aphasia as its primary ictal manifestation. Although psychiatric symptoms are uncommon in ASE, they may obscure the diagnosis when present. We report an atypical case, presenting predominantly with agitation and irritability, which was rapidly diagnosed as ASE by electroencephalography (EEG) based on the abrupt symptom onset and neurological history.

sections.heading: Case presentation
sections.text: A 49-year-old right-handed woman with alcohol use disorder was referred to our psychiatric hospital because of agitation, irritability, and disorganized thinking. Approximately 2 months before presentation to our hospital, she developed a generalized tonic-clonic seizure 3 days after sustaining a head injury. A left posterior fossa subdural hematoma was diagnosed, and burr-hole evacuation was performed at a general hospital. She continued rehabilitation; however, 6 days before admission to our hospital, she suddenly developed incoherent speech with agitation and irritability, prompting referral to our psychiatric hospital. Neurological examination revealed sensory aphasia. Given the history of brain injury and abrupt symptom onset, EEG was performed and demonstrated left-dominant periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges, confirming ASE. Antiseizure treatment resolved the EEG abnormalities and aphasia; however, aphasia, agitation, and irritability recurred with periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges. The symptoms improved with intravenous diazepam, and no recurrence was observed for >2 years following optimization of antiseizure medication.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: ASE may present predominantly with psychiatric symptoms and be misdiagnosed as a primary psychiatric disorder. Recognizing symptom chronology and epileptogenic background is essential for prompting EEG evaluation and early diagnosis.

items.title: Gendered pathways to adolescent mental health: An empirical assessment of a new conceptual framework.
items.authors: Alaze A, Hagen D, Schamberger T, Razum O, Miani C.

sections.text: Gender norms and roles are important determinants of physical and mental health in the key period of adolescence. Yet, the gendered pathways to mental health in adolescents are not fully understood. Using a conceptual framework for global adolescent mental health that we developed based on a Delphi process, we empirically investigated the associations between six gender-related constructs and adolescent mental health. We used an existing cross-sectional dataset from Ethiopia (2020) from the Gender and Adolescence: Global Evidence (GAGE) project to explore the associations between sex, gender norms, psychological competencies, gender attitudes, gender roles, with the latter two also serving as mediators, and psychological distress (GHQ-12), using Structural Equation Modelling (SEM). The SEM model contained measurements from 1,651 adolescents, including 901 girls and 750 boys, with a median age of 13 years. Out of 14 pathways tested, we found statistically significant associations between psychological competencies and psychological distress; sex and psychological distress; sex and gender attitudes; and between gender norms and psychological competencies, gender attitudes, and gender roles. Hence, the gender-related constructs were mostly associated with each other, rather than with psychological distress. The gender-related constructs were associated with each other rather than with psychological distress. The mechanisms underlying these relationships and a potential interplay of gender-related pathways require longitudinal investigation.

items.title: Tuning in: how interoception shapes body image across early adolescence.
items.authors: Von Mohr M, Donaghy R, Ainley V, Moore I, Agyemang A, Tsakiris M.
items.journal: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences
items.journal_abbrev: Philos Trans R Soc Lond B Biol Sci

sections.text: Early adolescence is a critical time marked by dynamic changes in physiology, appearance and social environment. These changes are also reflected in how adolescents perceive themselves, including their bodies. The transition through pubertal stages allows us to consider the development of the self from the perspective of how body perception, both from within and from the outside, changes. Although research in adults and post-puberty adolescents suggests that lower interoceptive accuracy is associated with greater body-image concerns, how these factors interact during puberty remains unknown. We tested a sample of 181 girls (ages 10-14 years) spanning across a broad range of pubertal stages, on measures of interoceptive accuracy and behavioural and self-report measures of body image. Lower interoceptive accuracy predicted greater body-image dissatisfaction. Moreover, this relationship was moderated by pubertal stage, showing that the protective effect of higher interoceptive accuracy against body-image dissatisfaction was stronger during more advanced stages of puberty. Our findings show that interoceptive influences extend from the basic multisensory integration to conscious attitudes about our body during a critical developmental period, highlighting the positive role that better interoception can play in mental health. This article is part of the discussion meeting issue 'From being to identity: analysis and synthesis of the self'.

We tested a sample of 181 girls (ages 10-14 years) spanning across a broad range of pubertal stages, on measures of interoceptive accuracy and behavioural and self-report measures of body image. Lower interoceptive accuracy predicted greater body-image dissatisfaction. Moreover, this relationship was moderated by pubertal stage, showing that the protective effect of higher interoceptive accuracy against body-image dissatisfaction was stronger during more advanced stages of puberty. Our findings show that interoceptive influences extend from the basic multisensory integration to conscious attitudes about our body during a critical developmental period, highlighting the positive role that better interoception can play in mental health. items.title: Drinking Status and Mental Health Symptoms Among First-Year Medical Students: A Cross-Sectional Chain Mediation Analysis of Health-Promoting Lifestyle and Sleep Quality.
items.authors: Shi C, Wang Z, Luo J, Zhao M.

sections.heading: Purpose
sections.text: The high prevalence of mental health symptoms among college students is a global public concern. However, the research on potential risk factors such as drinking remains insufficient. This study aimed to explore the association between drinking and mental health among college students, and examine the mediating roles of health-promoting lifestyle (HPL) and sleep quality.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A single-center cross-sectional survey was conducted among 2272 first-year students from a medical university in Shanghai, China. Drinking status, HPL (measured by HPLP-II), sleep quality (measured by PSQI), and mental health (measured by SCL-90) were assessed. Frequentist structural equation modeling (SEM) and Bayesian SEM were used to examine the mediating associations, adjusting for sociodemographic covariates.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Drinking status was significantly correlated with poorer HPL, worse sleep quality, and more psychological symptoms (all p values < 0.001). When HPLP-II score or PSQI score was included as a single mediator respectively, the indirect effects were 0.021 (p < 0.001) and 0.025 (p = 0.010), accounting for 24.1% and 28.7% of the total effect. When the HPLP-II and PSQI formed a chain mediation pathway, the indirect effect value was 0.023 (p < 0.001), accounting for 26.4% of the total effect. Exploratory analyses of the nine symptom dimensions plus the additional factor showed directionally consistent chain mediation associations, and a significant direct association was observed with somatization.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: HPL and sleep quality may be involved in the association between drinking and mental health symptoms and form a chain mediating association. These findings suggest that HPL and sleep quality may be potential targets for mental health promotion in college students.

items.title: Beyond Ethical Awareness: Knowledge-Application Gaps Among Nigerian Nursing and Midwifery Students in a Faith-Based Institution.
items.authors: Ochasi A, Okunna N, Ogu H, Isueseni SA, Agbagwa G, Obasi JC.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Recent studies document growing but uneven healthcare ethics education across Nigerian health professions programs. Relatively little is known about how nursing and midwifery students in faith-based institutions respond to clinical ethics vignettes spanning professional risk, contested moral norms, and care for stigmatized populations. This study examined ethical knowledge-application patterns among students at a faith-based nursing institution in Southeast Nigeria.

sections.heading: Objectives
sections.text: This study aimed to assess nursing and midwifery students' self-reported awareness of core ethical principles and professional obligations, examine their responses to vignette-based ethical dilemmas, and identify domain-specific patterns of divergence between self-reported ethical awareness and vignette-based ethical recognition and evaluation.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A cross-sectional survey was administered to 614 nursing and midwifery students who attended a one-day Healthcare Ethics Workshop at a private, Catholic-affiliated College of Nursing Sciences in Southeast Nigeria. A self-administered questionnaire assessed sociodemographic characteristics, prior ethics exposure, ethical awareness, and responses to ten clinical ethics vignettes involving whistleblowing, medical error disclosure, patient-provider boundaries, reporting of unethical practices, abortion, physician-assisted suicide, euthanasia, transgender care, conscientious objection, and end-of-life decision-making. Descriptive statistics summarized responses across domains.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Most participants reported prior formal ethics training, and the overall mean self-reported awareness score was 4.06 ± 0.39 on a five-point scale. Students responded most consistently to scenarios involving patient-provider relationships (85.4% correct assessment; 87.8% correct evaluation) and reporting of unethical practices (71.5%; 95.4%). Domain-specific variation was evident in whistleblowing (62.7%; 39.6%), end-of-life requests (46.3%; 64.2%), disclosure of medical errors (49.9%; 80.3%), and abortion (75.7%; 49.0%).

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Students demonstrated high self-reported awareness of foundational ethical principles, but vignette-based performance varied across domains, with distinct recognition-evaluation patterns in professionally risky and socioculturally contested dilemmas. These findings support longitudinal, case-based, and dialogical ethics education that addresses professional risk, institutional hierarchy, and contested moral issues within the sociocultural context of nursing practice.

items.title: Non-urgent emergency department utilization in adults: a systematic review of associated factors across diverse health systems.
items.authors: Zarei E, Safari M, Nematollahi MS.
items.journal: Scandinavian journal of trauma, resuscitation and emergency medicine
items.journal_abbrev: Scand J Trauma Resusc Emerg Med

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Non-urgent emergency department (ED) visits represent a growing global challenge with significant economic and operational consequences. Despite previous reviews, important gaps remain. No review has included all commonly used terms for non-urgent ED visits, recent evidence has not been synthesised, and factors related to patients, health systems, and care contexts have rarely been examined together. This systematic review aimed to identify and categorize factors associated with non-urgent ED visits in adults.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for articles published between January 2015 and May 2026. We included cross-sectional, cohort, and case-control studies that compared urgent and non-urgent ED visits and reported at least one associated factor. Quality assessment was performed using Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) checklists. Because of substantial heterogeneity in definitions, the findings were synthesised narratively.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Thirty-two studies from 21 countries were included. The proportion of non-urgent visits ranged from 1% to 82.4%, depending on the definition and measurement approach used. Five approaches were used to define non-urgent visits. The most common were triage-based (41%) and clinical judgment-based (28%). Associated factors were classified into three main categories: (1) demographic and socioeconomic (younger age, female sex, low income, lower education, non-native nationality); (2) access and health system (self-referral, arrival on foot, weekend visits, shorter distance to ED, lack of a family physician, public insurance); and (3) clinical and perceptual (non-specific diagnosis, musculoskeletal problems, mental health conditions, prior ED visit history, and patient perception of illness severity). The strongest associations were reported for frequent previous ED visits (aOR up to 82.13) and patients who perceived their illness as non-serious (aOR up to 21.03).

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Non-urgent ED visits are influenced by multiple individual, health system, and perceptual factors. The substantial heterogeneity in definitional approaches underscores the need for conceptual standardization. No single intervention is likely to reduce non-urgent ED visits. Effective strategies should strengthen primary care, improve insurance policies, increase public health education, and empower patients.

items.title: GABAergic inhibition of the nucleus reuniens stabilizes post-learning quiet states and enhances memory consolidation.
items.authors: Guemarez LM, Rico G, da Costa Souza A, Varela C.
items.journal: Sleep advances : a journal of the Sleep Research Society

sections.text: Quiet states provide a permissive context for processes that benefit from reduced engagement with the environment, such as memory consolidation, but the circuit mechanisms that stabilize these states remain unclear. The midline thalamic nucleus reuniens (RE) regulates hippocampal-cortical interactions during memory consolidation, but its role in stabilizing post-learning quiet states is unknown. Here, we tested the effects of RE inhibition on quiet-state stability and memory consolidation in freely behaving rats. Following object-place recognition training, rats received RE microinfusions of muscimol or vehicle and we monitored their behavior during the subsequent period. We found that RE inhibition increased the duration of quiet bouts and reduced bout fragmentation. Twenty-four hours later, muscimol-treated rats showed enhanced object-place recognition memory. These findings suggest that RE regulates the stability of quiet states that facilitate memory consolidation and provide a circuit mechanism linking thalamic inhibition, quiet states, and memory function.

items.title: Loneliness and burnout among doctors in a public academic hospital in South Africa.
items.authors: Kissoon S, Hoare J.
items.journal: The South African journal of psychiatry : SAJP : the journal of the Society of Psychiatrists of South Africa

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Loneliness is a subjective experience of emotional distress where individuals feel a lack of meaningful relational connections, and burnout results from chronic workplace stress. Doctors may be at increased risk, but there is a lack of data on the experience of loneliness and burnout among doctors in South Africa.

sections.heading: Aim
sections.text: This study aimed to assess the prevalence of loneliness, socio-demographic factors associated with loneliness and the association of loneliness with burnout in doctors working in a public academic hospital.

sections.heading: Setting
sections.text: Groote Schuur Hospital, Cape Town, South Africa.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A cross-sectional quantitative survey study was conducted with doctors of all grades. Validated scales for assessing loneliness (UCLA Loneliness Scale) and burnout (Maslach Burnout Inventory) were administered via the survey.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Of 188 doctors, 71% reported moderate to high loneliness. A statistically significant correlation was found between UCLA loneliness and MBI scores. Unmarried doctors were lonelier, and those without children experienced higher burnout. Loneliness and burnout risk were associated with doctors who were older, more experienced and those working longer hours.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: There is a high prevalence of both loneliness and burnout in doctors working in a public academic hospital in Cape Town.

sections.heading: Contribution
sections.text: Interventions aimed at improving burnout in public academic hospital settings may benefit from strategies to enhance social connections and belonging in our institutions.

items.title: Preoperative mental health predicts early satisfaction but not two-year knee-specific functional improvement after unicompartmental knee arthroplasty: an analysis of a robotic-assisted cohort.
items.authors: Ng Y, Lim JTE, Chan I, Goh EJW, Tay DKJ, Pang HN, Yeo SJ, Liow MHL.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Preoperative mental health is an important determinant of patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), but its influence in unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) remains poorly characterized. In this robotic-assisted UKA cohort, we determined the effect of poor preoperative mental health on PROMs at six months and two years, described the change in mental health after surgery, and whether preoperative mental health predicted satisfaction and expectation fulfilment.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Prospectively collected registry data on 241 consecutive robotic-assisted medial UKAs performed between 2017 and 2024 were reviewed. Of these, 121 formed the primary complete-case cohort, and patients were stratified by preoperative 36-item Short Form Health Survey (SF-36) Mental Component Summary (MCS) into poor mental health (MCS < 50, n = 51) and good mental health (MCS ≥ 50, n = 70). Outcomes included the Knee Society Function and Knee Score (KSFS & KSKS) and Oxford Knee Score (OKS), SF-36 Physical Component Summary (PCS), satisfaction, and expectation fulfillment. Multivariable logistic regression identified predictors of satisfaction, expectation fulfilment, and mental health recovery.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Mean preoperative MCS was 41.2 in the low-MCS group and 58.2 in the high-MCS group (p < 0.001), with the former achieving greater MCS improvement at six months and two years (p < 0.05). Despite a lower preoperative KSKS and a higher (worse) OKS (p < 0.05) in the low-MCS group, both groups demonstrated comparable improvements in KSFS, KSKS, and OKS. However, divergent global physical recovery was observed at two years, with the high-MCS group achieving greater improvements in the SF-36 PCS compared to the low-MCS group (Δ 17.0 versus 11.1, p = 0.006; MCID attainment 85.7% versus 66.7%, p = 0.024; ANCOVA-adjusted p = 0.002). At six months, satisfaction (82.4 versus 97.1%; p = 0.008) and expectation fulfillment (70.6 versus 90.0%; p = 0.008) were significantly lower in the low-MCS group, while no difference was detected at two years. In exploratory subgroup analysis, persistently low MCS patients had significantly worse two-year PROMs than the high-MCS group. Preoperative MCS independently predicted six-month satisfaction (OR 1.078; p = 0.005) and expectation fulfillment (OR 1.061; p = 0.005). Among low-MCS patients, six-month MCS was associated with two-year mental health normalization (OR 1.083; p = 0.008), with an internally derived cutoff of MCS ≥ 53 (area under the curve [AUC], 0.783).

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Within this robotic-assisted UKA cohort, patients with poor preoperative mental health reported lower early satisfaction, but still achieved meaningful mental health recovery and knee-specific functional gains comparable to those with better preoperative mental health by two years, with no detectable difference in satisfaction at two years. Poor preoperative mental health should not preclude appropriately selected patients from undergoing UKA. The six-month MCS is an internally derived exploratory signal that may help identify patients warranting closer monitoring.

items.title: Assessment of unsuppressed viral load and its determinants among pregnant and breastfeeding women living with HIV in the prevention of vertical transmission programme in Bugesera District, Rwanda, 2023.
items.authors: Ndabana D, Uwamahoro B, Mukamurigo J.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Prevention of vertical transmission (PVT) of HIV programs are designed to prevent the transmission of HIV during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Nevertheless, attaining viral suppression among mothers living with HIV remains a major challenge, especially in resource-constrained settings like Bugesera District, Rwanda. This study aim to determine the prevalence and determinants of unsuppressed viral load (VL) among pregnant and breastfeeding women living with HIV enrolled in the PVT of HIV program as of 2023.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: An analytical cross-sectional study using retrospective record review was carried out using secondary data from 508 pregnant and breastfeeding women living with HIV enrolled in the PVT of HIV services in 15 health centres in Bugesera District between January 2023 and December 2023, Data were extracted from patient records and analysed using descriptive statistics, bivariate analysis, and multivariate logistic regression to identify factors associated with an unsuppressed VL (≥ 200 copies/mL).

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Among the 508 pregnant and breastfeeding women living with HIV enrolled in the PVT of HIV services, the prevalence of unsuppressed VL was 8.5% (95% CI: 6.3-11.2). factors associated with unsuppressed VL were mental health problems (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 4.7, 95% CI: 2.3-9.5, p < 0.001), low attendance to antenatal care (ANC) (< 4 visits) (aOR = 2.2, 95% CI: 1.1-4.7, p = 0.025), a history of treatment interruption (aOR = 2.4, 95% CI: 1.1-4.9, p = 0.015) and being married or cohabiting (aOR = 2.0, 95% CI: 1.0-4.1, p = 0.035).

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: The unsuppression viral load rate among women living with HIV in Bugesera District was high. This study highlights the need of strengthening psychosocial support, increase attendance of antenatal care consultations and improve antiretroviral (ART) retention in the PVT of HIV program, particularly among women who are partnered.

items.title: The German emotion beliefs questionnaire: factorial validity, measurement invariance, and descriptive reference values in a population-representative sample.
items.authors: Lammers JR, Brähler E, Koechel A, Conrad R, Ramm M.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Beliefs about emotions are considered a central mechanism of emotion regulation and mental health [1]. The 16-item Emotion Beliefs Questionnaire (EBQ; [2]) assesses beliefs about the usefulness and controllability of positive and negative emotions. While the original study supported a three-factor model, subsequent population-based studies favored the theoretically proposed four-factor structure. Although two German-language adaptations exist, neither has been validated in a population-representative sample, and descriptive reference values, evidence for measurement invariance across key sociodemographic groups, and systematic investigations of sociodemographic correlates of emotion beliefs are still lacking.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: The German version of the EBQ [3] was administered to a representative sample of the German general population (N = 2368; mean age = 50.3; SD = 17.13; range: 18-93; 44.7% men, 55.2% women). Confirmatory factor analyses (MLR) were conducted to compare competing three- and four-factor models. Measurement invariance across gender, age, and educational level was examined and descriptive reference values were calculated.

sections.heading: Results

items.title: Knowledge of and preferred legal grounds for abortion in Kenya: a national cross-sectional telephone survey.
items.authors: Juma K, Mutuku E, Athero S, Akuku I, Ajayi AI, Ushie BA.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Inadequate knowledge of abortion law in restrictive settings impedes women's access to safe services and engenders poor abortion perception and stigma among the general population. There is limited understanding of the public's knowledge and support for abortion in Kenya. This study aimed to assess public knowledge of the current abortion law, factors associated with accurate knowledge, and to characterize the preferred conditions under which abortion should be legally permitted in Kenya.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: We conducted a nationwide cross-sectional survey using mobile phones to collect data from adults aged 18 or older. The sample was drawn from a database maintained by a mobile survey provider, with over 12 million telephone numbers across Kenya. We used a random digit dialing approach to select and recruit participants. Trained research assistants administered telephonic interviews using a structured questionnaire that had questions assessing knowledge of conditions for legally sanctioned abortion and legal conditions under which they would support abortion. We summarized continuous variables into means (standard deviations) and medians (interquartile range), while categorical variables (including for the outcomes) as proportions. We performed a survey-weighted quasi-Poisson regression model to assess associations between sociodemographic variables (such as age, sex, marital status, education among others) and the knowledge levels of abortion laws. We also conducted latent class analysis to characterize the preferred legal grounds around abortion by the Kenyan population.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Of the 8,942 respondents, 76%, 74%, and 33% knew that the Kenyan law permits abortion when a woman's life or health is at risk and when the pregnancy results from rape, respectively. Relative to males, females had 2% higher knowledge of abortion law (score ratio 1.02; 95% CI: 1.01-1.03), while those with secondary and university education were associated with 6% (score ratio 1.06; 95% CI: 1.01-1.12) and 8% (score ratio 1.08; 95% CI: 1.03-1.14) higher knowledge of abortion law respectively, compared to those with no education. Most respondents indicated support for abortion when a woman's life (71%), health (64%), or mental health (43%) is at risk. About one-third would support abortions when pregnancy results from rape (29%) or incest (28%). The latent class analysis showed that most respondents (41%) preferred legalization of abortion for health and life reasons, whereas 30% opposed legalization of abortion under any circumstances.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: While knowledge of some legal grounds for abortion in Kenya is relatively high, important gaps remain, particularly regarding abortion following rape. Public support for abortion largely aligns with life- and health-related grounds, although a substantial proportion oppose abortion under any circumstances. Targeted dissemination of accurate information on abortion law is needed to address knowledge gaps and support informed public dialogue and policy engagement.

items.title: Progressive Ataxia and Cognitive Impairment Associated With SEZ6L2: Serum Neurofilament Light Chain as a Biomarker of Disease Activity.
items.authors: Fazio C, Regalbuto S, Arceri S, Comolli D, Calculli A, Trobbiani G, Battaglia G, Zuliani F, Gastaldi M, Pisani A.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Autoimmune encephalitis (AE) associated with SEZ6L2 antibodies is a rare neurological disorder characterized by subacute onset of cerebellar ataxia, cognitive dysfunction, and extrapyramidal features. Few cases have been reported, and data on long-term course and treatment response remain limited.

sections.heading: Case presentation
sections.text: A 64-year-old woman developed progressive cerebellar ataxia, cognitive decline, and psychiatric symptoms starting insidiously after SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia in September 2022. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis almost 1 year after onset were unremarkable. Due to progressive symptoms, she was admitted to our department in December 2024. Examination showed severe truncal and gait ataxia, memory impairment, and prominent frontal-executive dysfunction. Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral hippocampal T2 hyperintensity with severe medial temporal lobe and cerebellar atrophy. Neuronal antibody testing with a tissue-based assay (TBA) optimized for surface antigens showed strong neuropilar hippocampal and cerebellar staining in serum and CSF. A specific live cell-based assay (CBA) confirmed that the reactivity could be attributed to SEZ6L2 antibodies. Plasmapheresis and high-dose corticosteroids resulted in stabilization of gait impairment and mild cognitive improvement. Longitudinal plasma neurofilament light chain (NFL) monitoring showed initially high levels (85.12 pg/mL), followed by a drastic reduction some months after immunotherapy.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: AE can mimic neurodegenerative processes, and SEZ6L2 antibody testing should be considered in patients with progressive ataxia and limbic involvement, even when no additional clues point towards an autoimmune etiology. Notably, the condition manifested a partial response to immunotherapy, supported by NFL reduction. This suggests that NFL might represent a useful biomarker to monitor disease activity in these conditions.

items.title: Physical medicine and rehabilitation clinics as transitional care hubs after stroke.
items.authors: Baratta JM, Harr E, Cardoza K, Jackson M, Bettger JP.

sections.text: The transition from hospital-based care to community living is a vulnerable period for stroke survivors and caregivers. During this period, patients often experience evolving medical, functional, psychosocial, and social needs while navigating fragmented systems of care. Although guidelines emphasize timely post-discharge follow-up, coordinated discharge planning, rehabilitation continuity, and linkage to primary care and community resources, there remains no consistently implemented model for delivering transitional care after stroke. Outpatient Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (PM&R) clinics are well positioned to address this gap because physiatrists routinely manage post-stroke disability, functional recovery, secondary complications, therapy coordination, equipment needs, caregiver concerns, and barriers to community reintegration. This Perspective proposes a PM&R-based bridge clinic model for selected stroke survivors discharged home from acute care or inpatient rehabilitation settings, particularly those without established primary care or with barriers to timely outpatient follow-up. In this model, a small interdisciplinary core team, including a rehabilitation physician, advanced practice provider, and social worker or care coordinator, provides time-limited post-discharge follow-up focused on medical, mental health, and functional stabilization, medication reconciliation, rehabilitation planning, durable medical equipment needs, social drivers of health, caregiver support, and primary care linkage. By embedding transitional care within existing outpatient rehabilitation infrastructure, PM&R-based bridge clinics may offer a practical and scalable approach to strengthening continuity across the post-stroke care continuum.

items.title: Effects of exercise interventions on executive function in adolescents: a systematic review and three-level meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
items.authors: Li D, Li S, Yao M, Ye S, Geng K, Zhou L, Niu L.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: To estimate the effects of exercise interventions lasting at least 4 weeks on overall executive function and its three domains in adolescents, and to explore differences across population subgroups.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Nine databases were systematically searched. Individually randomized parallel-group trials of adolescents aged 10-19 years comparing exercise with no additional structured exercise were included. Dependent Hedges' g estimates were synthesized using three-level models with approximate within-trial covariance and trial-clustered CR2 inference. Risk of bias and evidence certainty were assessed using RoB 2 and GRADE.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Twenty-two independent trials (1,599 unique participants) contributed 27 comparisons and 86 effect sizes. The pooled overall EF effect favored exercise (g = 0.55, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.77; p < 0.001), with substantial total heterogeneity (I² = 84.92%). Domain-specific estimates also favored exercise: inhibitory control (17 trials; g = 0.56, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.84), working memory (10 trials; g = 0.51, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.84), and cognitive flexibility (nine trials; g = 0.43, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.57). The overall estimate was more heavily informed by inhibitory-control scores (47/86) than by working-memory (25/86) or cognitive-flexibility scores (14/86). Correlation, trial-exclusion, risk-of-bias, and task-classification sensitivity analyses retained effects in the same direction. Certainty was low for overall EF, inhibitory control, and working memory, and moderate for cognitive flexibility.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Sustained exercise may improve performance on EF tasks in adolescents, but heterogeneous interventions and controls, overlapping task constructs, and mostly low-certainty evidence limit the generality and real-world interpretation of the pooled effects.

items.title: Beyond time spent online: exploring functional motives, discourse-related self-appraisals, and social media addiction-like symptoms.
items.authors: Lehenbauer-Baum M, Klaps A, Kovacovsky Z, Stetina BU.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Research has increasingly examined excessive social media (SM) use in relation to negative mental health outcomes, often conceptualized as SM "addiction" or "problematic use", and assessed using self-report scales such as the Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale (BSMAS). While the BSMAS assesses self-reported addiction-like symptoms, scores may be associated not only with time spent using SM, but also with the functions SM serves and discourse-related self-appraisals through which individuals evaluate their own use. This exploratory pilot study examined these dimensions.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: We developed two exploratory instruments assessing functional motives and discourse-related self-appraisals. A convenience sample of 291 SM users completed the BSMAS, SM use questions, and both instruments. Exploratory factor analyses, correlations and hierarchical regressions examined associations with BSMAS scores. Three sensitivity analyses examined potential conceptual overlap with BSMAS item content.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The Functional SM Use Survey yielded five domains: emotional self-regulatory engagement and escapism, global wellbeing benefit, entertainment and stimulation-driven engagement, instrumental and goal-directed use, and social validation and self-presentation. The Discourse-Based Survey yielded three domains: socially driven self-judgment, warning-triggered self-appraisal, and perceived over-pathologization and normative dissent. Weekly SM use was significantly associated with BSMAS scores in Step 1 but no longer significant in the fully adjusted model. Emotional self-regulatory engagement and escapism (β = 0.438) and warning-triggered self-appraisal (β = 0.273) remained statistically significant; the model explained 49.8% of the variance. The socially driven self-judgment association weakened after removing overlapping items, whereas the warning-triggered self-appraisal association changed minimally after removal of the BSMAS work/study-impact item. This does not establish conceptual independence between warning-triggered self-appraisal and perceived problematic use. Removing the BSMAS mood-modification item attenuated, but did not eliminate, the emotional self-regulatory engagement and escapism association.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: BSMAS scores were associated with reported SM use, coping-oriented motives and discourse-related self-appraisals. Sensitivity findings indicate that some associations were attenuated after removing overlapping evaluative content, whereas others changed minimally after targeted item removal. These analyses do not establish conceptual independence among the measures. These exploratory findings indicate associations between self-reported addiction-like symptoms, SM motives and discourse-related self-appraisals, but the conceptual distinctiveness of the newly proposed domains requires independent validation.

items.title: Geographical Distribution of Exposure to Fires in the United States Between 2004 and 2023.
items.authors: Sakka R, Pu Q, Sahar L, Nogueira LM, Liu Y.

sections.text: Fire activity is increasing across the United States. Proximity to fires poses health risks beyond smoke exposure including injury, mental health impacts, and contamination of water and soil. However, the predominance of smoke-focused studies has contributed to public health strategies centered on mitigating smoke exposure. This study aims to characterize geographic patterns of population-weighted fire burden to inform public health and fire management. Population-weighted fire-day burden (person days) were calculated for each census tract and year by multiplying the tract population by number of days with at least one satellite-detected active fire. This metric captures the frequency of detected fire presence, including recurrent smaller fires, rather than smoke, fire intensity, or fire severity. These measures were summarized nationally, by region, and by demographic groups. Temporal trends between 2004 and 2023 were evaluated using regression models, and region-specific percentiles identified census tracts with fire days in the 99th percentile every year (i.e., consistently high). Between 2004 and 2023, there were 9.12 billion population-weighted fire-days in the United States, 64% of which occurred in the South. Population-weighted fire burden increased significantly over the study period nationally and in most census tracts. Census tracts with persistently high fire-day burden were concentrated in Florida, consistent with regions where frequent agricultural burning occurs. Population-weighted fire burden is disproportionately high among individuals residing in the South, highlighting the importance of tailoring strategies for mitigating the health risks of fires to local fire practices to protect the health and safety of residents in the region.

items.title: A call for action: Guidelines for implementation of mental health services at the community level.
items.authors: Thobane KF, Mulaudzi FM, Lavhelani NR, Gundo R.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Mental health challenges account for approximately 18% of global disease burden. Few people with mental health challenges receive the required treatment, especially at community level. Implementation of mental health services at the community level is vital.

sections.heading: Aim
sections.text: The study aimed to explore and describe the content for inclusion in the guidelines for the implementation of mental health services in the Ward-Based Primary Health Care Outreach Teams (WBPHCOTs) services in South Africa.

sections.heading: Setting
sections.text: Data was collected in subdistrict one offices from the experts in mental health services and WBPHCOTs working in Tshwane District, Gauteng province, South Africa.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A qualitative, explorative and descriptive design that followed a Nominal Group Technique (NGT) for data collection. Eleven experts were purposively sampled for participation in the study. The NGT process was followed: silent generation of ideas, round robin, group discussion and clarification process. Finally, ranking of ideas and group consensus was reached.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The following content was identified for inclusion in the guidelines: visits to households, collaboration with mental health key stakeholders, training, mental health prevention and promotion, adherence to treatment and advocacy, mental health professionals' support, and strengthening community mental health services.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: The study assisted in identifying the content to be included in the guidelines for the implementation of mental health services in the WBPHCOTs' services.

sections.heading: Contribution
sections.text: This study provides the content that could be included in the development of the guidelines for the implementation of mental health services in the WBPHCOTs services, with the anticipated contribution to the improvement in the implementation of mental health services at community level.

items.title: Barriers and enablers of work-life balance among regulatory affairs pharmacists working remotely in Gauteng, South Africa: A qualitative study.
items.authors: Sekgalakane KM, Hlungwani TM, Orchard A.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Regulatory Affairs (RA) pharmacists in South Africa transitioned to remote work during the COVID-19 pandemic and continued post-restrictions. Limited research on their work-life balance (WLB) experiences hinders supportive workplace policy development and understanding of work-family conflict dynamics to inform sustainable remote work practices.

sections.heading: Aim
sections.text: This study aimed to explore the WLB experiences of RA pharmacists following the easing of COVID-19 restrictions.

sections.heading: Setting
sections.text: The study was conducted in Gauteng province, South Africa.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: An exploratory qualitative design used semi-structured interviews guided by Bronfenbrenner's framework and the Work-Life Harmony model. Data from 17 participants were analysed thematically using inductive and deductive approaches.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The WLB barriers and enablers emerged across socio-ecological levels. The microsystem included boundary challenges, overwork, isolation and adaptive routines. The mesosystem reflected family support, work-life enrichment and competing demands. Exosystem factors, including micromanagement, inconsistent policy implementation and limited resources, undermined flexibility and autonomy, while supportive management and peer collaboration enhanced WLB. Macrosystem regulatory demands, time-zone pressures and an output-driven culture extended working hours. The chronosystem reflected evolving work arrangements and boundary-setting.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Remote and hybrid work increased flexibility, family engagement and reduced commuting for RA pharmacists. However, blurred boundaries, overtime, constant availability, micromanagement, inconsistent policies, staffing shortages and poor support undermined autonomy and mental health.

sections.heading: Contribution
sections.text: The study provides unique insights into WLB barriers and enablers among RA pharmacists, informing management strategies and psychological support for remote work optimisation.

items.title: Development and Early Implementation of a Parent Peer Programme for Rural and Remote Communities: An Evaluation of Feasibility and Acceptability.
items.authors: Gillespie KM, McClenaghan M, Branjerdporn N, Jockel S, Branjerdporn G.
items.journal: Health expectations : an international journal of public participation in health care and health policy

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: The aim of this study was to evaluate the acceptability and feasibility of a Parent Peer support programme in rural and remote Queensland to support parents and improve mental wellbeing, and to describe programme co-design and implementation.

sections.heading: Setting
sections.text: Central Queensland.

sections.heading: Participants
sections.text: Parent Peers and project stakeholders involved in the co-design, development, and implementation of a rural and remote Parent Peer support programme.

sections.heading: Design
sections.text: A mixed-methods study using online surveys and interviews explored the co-design, implementation, and perceptions of a Peer Support programme for parents in four rural and remote Queensland communities and a Parent Peer training programme. Seven Parent Peers and 13 stakeholders provided perspectives on the co-design process and the implementation of the Parent Peer programme. Parent Peers also provided feedback on the Peer Support training modules. Descriptive statistics and thematic and summative content analysis were used to analyse and describe quantitative and qualitative data.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Two themes were identified, including 'Connection and Collaboration', which identified the collaborative, co‑design process as crucial for the successful development, implementation, and sustainability of the programme; and 'An Evolving Role', which acknowledged the importance of the evolving and adaptable nature of the role to ensure tailored and responsive strategies for individual communities. Training was acceptable and engaging for Parent Peers, providing them with valuable education and support as they began their role.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: The co-designed Parent Peer programme was feasible, acceptable, and strongly supported by participants. The Parent Peer role needed to be flexible and adaptable to meet changing and unique community needs. The Parent Peer model could be widely implemented in rural and remote communities across Australia to improve parent support and wellbeing.

sections.heading: Patient or public contribution
sections.text: An iterative consultative co-design process was systematically followed throughout. Organisational healthcare professionals,individuals with lived experience, parents, early education specialists, and community stakeholders were actively involved in the design, development, and implementation of the Parent Peer project.
