items.title: Beyond Clinical Stability: Recovery and Reintegration Among Residents of a Psychiatric Halfway Home in India- A Qualitative Study.
items.authors: Poornachandrika A, Subramaniam S, Mariadharshini R, Puthalath M, Thomas MM.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Halfway homes provide transitional support for persons with mental illness moving from institutional care to community living. However, there is limited evidence from India on how residents experience recovery and rehabilitation within these settings. Hence, this study was done to explore the lived experiences of persons with mental illness residing in a halfway home, understand its role in rehabilitation and recovery, and identify factors influencing rehabilitation outcomes.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A qualitative study was conducted among residents of a government-run halfway home. Data were collected through in-depth interviews with eight purposively selected residents who had lived in the facility. Interviews explored experiences of rehabilitation, daily functioning, social relationships, occupational engagement, future aspirations, and barriers to reintegration. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke's approach.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Five themes emerged: transition from institutional dependence to everyday autonomy; work, routine, and reconstruction of identity; relearning daily living and functional independence; social support, family estrangement, and reintegration challenges; and hope and future aspirations. Participants described halfway home as a space that promoted autonomy, privacy, mobility, and participation in everyday life. Work and structured routines contributed to identity reconstruction and purpose. Recovery was facilitated by peer and institutional support, while stigma, family estrangement, and medication-related challenges remained important barriers.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Halfway homes play a vital role in promoting recovery, autonomy, and community reintegration among persons with mental illness and represent an important component of recovery-oriented mental health services in India.

items.title: Climate, Air Quality, and Emergency Department Use in Northern Germany: Protocol for a Multicenter Register Study.
items.authors: Jagomast T, Raddatz M, Penner L, Lüthgen M, Ristau P, Dersch W, Wallis S, Sayk F, Metzner J, Wolfrum S, Calero Valdez A, Baron A, Kerner T, Grzegorzek M, Schmidtke C, Drömann D, Watz H, Weckmann M, Weckmann M, Brinkmann F, Franzen KF.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Climate change threatens population health through temperature extremes, air pollution, and altered infectious disease patterns. Emergency departments (EDs) are sensitive indicators of climate-related health impacts; however, comprehensive multicenter investigations integrating meteorological factors, air quality, and infectious disease surveillance across different health care provision levels remain scarce in Germany, particularly in maritime climate regions.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: This study aims to characterize the impact of meteorological factors, air quality, and infectious disease dynamics on ED presentations across multiple health care facilities and care provision levels in northern Germany over an 11-year period.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This retrospective, multicenter, observational study will examine ED presentations across 4 facilities representing different care provision levels in the greater Lübeck area and southeastern Schleswig-Holstein, Germany, from January 2014 to December 2024. Clinical data, including ICD ( International Classification of Diseases )-coded diagnoses, patient demographics, and temporal information, will be linked with meteorological data from the German Weather Service, air quality measurements from state environmental monitoring, and infectious disease surveillance from the Robert Koch Institute. The primary outcomes will be daily ED visits overall and stratified by disease category (cardiovascular, respiratory, psychiatric, infectious, renal, neurological, and surgical/traumatic). Distributed lag nonlinear models within a generalized additive modeling framework will be used to characterize temperature-health relationships, accounting for delayed and nonlinear effects, and adjusted for temporal trends, seasonality, and infectious disease incidence. Subgroup analyses will examine vulnerable populations by age, sex, and socioeconomic status.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Project planning and conceptualization began in June 2024, and ethical approval was granted in July 2025. Following approval, clinical data were transferred sequentially across participating sites in July 2025, August 2025, and October 2025. Data from 3 of the 4 participating hospitals have been successfully received, while the final outstanding dataset is expected in the second half of 2026. Meteorological data collection was completed in October 2025 and air quality data in January 2026. While preliminary descriptive statistical analyses have already commenced, inferential statistics will be performed once data collection is fully completed.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: This multicenter study will provide systematic evidence on climate-sensitive ED utilization in a maritime climate region of northern Germany. By integrating clinical, meteorological, air quality, and infectious disease data across 4 hospitals of varying care complexity, the study is well positioned to characterize nonlinear and delayed health effects of temperature extremes across a broad spectrum of acute conditions. Results are expected to inform regional health care capacity planning, early warning systems, and public health preparedness, while contributing to the broader evidence base on climate and health.

items.title: Catatonia knowledge in medical practitioners from low-resource settings.
items.authors: Kaddu AK, Saina DC, Morawej Z, Ssembajjwe W, Ssemata AS, Ndigamanya RI, van der Walt K, Kalungi A, Akena D, Nakasujja N, Mwesiga EK.
items.journal: The South African journal of psychiatry : SAJP : the journal of the Society of Psychiatrists of South Africa

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Catatonia is a neuropsychiatric emergency that requires rapid intervention to prevent complications. It is unclear whether African medical practitioners have the requisite knowledge to identify and manage catatonia.

sections.heading: Aim
sections.text: To examine knowledge of catatonia among medical practitioners across partnering institutions of the African Catatonia Registry (ACR), a multi-country resource for research in Africa.

sections.heading: Setting
sections.text: The study was conducted among medical practitioners across the ACR partnering institutions.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: The study was a descriptive, cross-sectional online survey comprising 63 questions to examine knowledge of catatonia. Responses were scored with a positive mark if correct and a negative mark if wrong, then standardised and dichotomised to indicate low or sufficient knowledge.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Out of 321 participants, nearly half (46.7%) were psychiatrists, and 50.8% had sufficient knowledge of catatonia. Multivariate analysis showed that knowledge varied by sub-domain, country, specialty and prior experience with catatonia. Specialisation in psychiatry was significantly associated with sufficient knowledge of classification (adjusted risk ratio [aRR] 2.15 [95% confidence intervals {CI}: 1.35-3.43]), diagnostic symptoms (aRR = 3.30 [95% CI: 1.62-6.69]), screening (aRR = 4.72 [95% CI: 2.25-9.91]) and rating scales (aRR = 3.34 [95% CI: 1.32-8.46]). Prior experience with catatonia was also associated with sufficient knowledge across these areas (all p ≤ 0.05).

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: While knowledge of catatonia and its diagnostic criteria is sufficient among practitioners, knowledge of its symptoms, treatment and complication management remains low.

sections.heading: Contribution
sections.text: The study highlights the need for the ACR to promote improvements in the identification and management of catatonia to achieve better patient outcomes.

items.title: Utilisation of coercive measures in involuntary patients admitted to two psychiatric hospitals in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa.
items.authors: Mashaphu S, Shozi ZP, Ntlantsana V, Saloojee S.
items.journal: The South African journal of psychiatry : SAJP : the journal of the Society of Psychiatrists of South Africa

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: There is a high prevalence of involuntary psychiatric admissions in South Africa, with literature on the measures used to coerce patients into care being limited.

sections.heading: Aim
sections.text: This study aimed to quantify the coercive measures that were used during involuntary admissions to two psychiatric hospitals in KwaZulu-Natal province, and to identify factors associated with their use.

sections.heading: Setting
sections.text: King Dinuzulu Hospital Complex in Durban and Townhill Psychiatric Hospital in Pietermaritzburg.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This was a sub-analysis of a cross-sectional, descriptive, quantitative study of involuntarily admitted patients aged 18 years and above. Data were collected through participant interviews at discharge and by extracting information from patients' clinical records and Mental Health Care Act forms.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Of the 131 patients included, 66% were male, 85.5% were single, and 71.4% were unemployed. The prevalence of chemical, mechanical, physical restraint, and seclusion was 73.3%, 14.5%, 24.43%, and 16.8%, respectively, with 38.2% being exposed to more than one method. Significantly more male patients than female patients were physically restrained h(81% vs 19%; p = 0.04), and placed in seclusion (86.4% vs 13.6%; p = 0.05). Except for mechanical restraint, a longer length of hospital stay was significantly associated with the other three coercive measures ( p ≤ 0.05).

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Chemical restraint was the most common method of coercion, with more than one-third of patients being exposed to two or more methods.

sections.heading: Contribution
sections.text: This study highlights the high utilisation of coercive methods and informs the need for reducing their use in psychiatric hospitals in South Africa.

items.title: Family cohesion and adolescent self-esteem: mediating effects of interpersonal self-support and moderating role of school attachment.
items.authors: Yao Z, Luo Y.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Adolescent mental health is a pressing global concern, and in collectivist societies such as China, family and school contexts are particularly influential. This study examined whether interpersonal self-support mediates the association between family cohesion and self-esteem among Chinese adolescents and whether school attachment moderates the first stage of that mediation pathway.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 728 adolescents (mean age = 13.81 years, SD = 0.91, range 12-16; 44.0% male) from five public junior high schools in Hunan Province, China. Confirmatory factor analyses were conducted in Mplus 8.3, and the moderated mediation model was tested with Hayes' PROCESS macro (Model 7) in SPSS 27 using observed variables and 5,000 bootstrap samples.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Family cohesion was positively associated with self-esteem and with interpersonal self-support, and interpersonal self-support partially mediated the family cohesion-self-esteem association. School attachment moderated the first stage of the mediation pathway, b = 0.076, 95% CI [0.024, 0.128], Δ R ^2 =.008: the positive association between family cohesion and interpersonal self-support was significant at all levels of school attachment and was stronger among adolescents reporting higher school attachment, and the conditional indirect effect increased from 0.107 at low to 0.153 at high school attachment.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: The indirect pathway was secondary to the direct association between family cohesion and self-esteem, and the moderation effect was modest. Because the design was cross-sectional and self-reported, these associations should not be interpreted causally. The findings suggest that schools may support the benefits of family cohesion for adolescent self-esteem by strengthening teacher-student relationships and cultivating a sense of belonging.

items.title: Predicting behavioral escalation in students with autism using physiological and movement data.
items.authors: Lamb R, Owens T, Choi I, Kundu S, Nookkarapu S, Ray P, Kavner A.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Behavioral escalation in students with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) presents significant challenges in educational and community settings, often leading to reactive interventions after behaviors become observable. This study investigated whether physiological and movement data obtained from wearable biometric sensors could retrospectively identify precursors of escalation and inform proactive support strategies.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Physiological and movement data were collected from 30 students with ASD in naturalistic classroom environments using wearable sensors. Measures included heart rate variability (HRV), galvanic skin response (GSR), skin temperature, and accelerometer data. Behavioral observations were used to identify escalation events, and machine learning models, including Random Forest, Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, were trained on previously collected physiological and behavioral data to classify pre-escalation states. Model performance was evaluated retrospectively rather than through real-time deployment.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Among the models tested, the LSTM network achieved the highest classification accuracy (85.2%) in identifying pre-escalation states. Physiological changes associated with escalation were detectable approximately 2 to 5 minutes before observable behavioral manifestations. HRV and GSR emerged as the strongest predictive features, while inclusion of accelerometer data further improved classification performance. These findings suggest that measurable physiological patterns precede overt behavioral escalation in students with ASD.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: The results support the feasibility of using wearable biometric data and machine learning approaches to retrospectively identify antecedent physiological markers of behavioral escalation. Interpreted through frameworks drawn from Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) and Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), these physiological signals may function as both antecedents to challenging behavior and indicators of internal emotional or regulatory states. Although real-time implementation was not evaluated, the findings provide a foundation for future predictive monitoring systems designed to facilitate earlier intervention, reduce reliance on reactive or punitive responses, and promote more inclusive and emotionally responsive educational environments for neurodiverse learners.

items.title: Insomnia severity and multidimensional psychological well-being in Chilean correctional personnel: a cross-sectional study.
items.authors: Benjumeda Wynhoven I, Varela Sepúlveda S, Bravo Lara RB, Ocampo Vélez G.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Prison officers in Chile work under highly stressful and dangerous conditions characterized by prison overcrowding, violence, long shifts, and chronic exposure to stress. Shift work and irregular schedules negatively affect sleep quality and contribute to insomnia, which in turn may impair psychological well-being. Despite growing evidence on occupational stress in correctional staff, limited research has examined the relationship between sleep quality, insomnia, and psychological well-being in prison guards. Therefore, this study aimed to assess working conditions, subjective sleep quality, insomnia severity, and psychological well-being among Chilean prison officers.

sections.text: Participants reported low institutional support (60.5%) and frequent sick leave (68.4%). items.title: Felt needs of undergraduate and postgraduate psychiatry teachers in India: Cross-sectional survey across institutes of National Importance (INI) and Non-INIs.
items.authors: Singh S, Naskar I, Jangra J, Verma P, Pal A, Verma N, Kadarappa KK, Rao KM.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: With the implementation of competency-based medical education by the National Medical Commission (NMC), understanding the perceived needs of undergraduate (UG) and postgraduate (PG) psychiatry teachers across Institutes of National Importance (INIs) and non-INIs is essential.

sections.heading: Aim
sections.text: To assess and compare the felt needs of medical teachers of psychiatry at INIs and non-INIs in India.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: An online survey was conducted among UG and PG psychiatry teachers across India. The survey questionnaire assessed teaching practices, NMC curriculum adherence, and felt training needs.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: A total of 214 valid responses were collected (response rate: 33.7%), out of which 128 participants were from INIs. About 82% respondents felt that there was a need for training in UG and PG psychiatry teaching. Adherence to the NMC curriculum was reported by about 64% and 54% UG and PG teachers, respectively. About 33% respondents had received some prior formal training in medical education. Faculty members were more likely than senior residents to have received prior formal training (65.4% vs. 12.8%, P < 0.001). Among PG teaching methods, case-based learning (74.3%), seminars (72.9%), and journal clubs (70.6%) were most common, whereas UG teaching relied on didactic lectures (61.2%), case-based learning (54.2%), and small group discussions (50.0%). There was no significant difference between felt needs of INI and non-INI respondents, except for higher PG teaching involvement in non-INIs ( P < 0.001).

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: There is an unmet need for structured faculty development in psychiatry teaching at both INIs and non-INIs. Targeted, competency-based training programs, especially for senior residents, are needed to strengthen psychiatry education in India.

items.title: Developing and evaluating a customized evidence-based safety training program for healthcare staff: a quality improvement approach.
items.authors: Lin E, Boyd H, Bratsalis E, Hodgson K, Islam F, Khan MI, Crestois N, Sockalingam S.

sections.text: The high risk of workplace violence (WPV) for workers in mental health care settings and the potentially serious impacts, both mental and physical, have prompted many hospitals to mandate behavioral safety skills training for their staff. There are, however, some considerable challenges to delivering this type of training. First, while there are international and national/regional guidelines for mitigating WPV, the evaluation literature does not provide consistent guidance on which training methods are the most effective across a range of settings. Second, hospitals differ in terms of their objectives and their identified safety issues suggesting that a tailored approach rather than a one-size-fits-all training would be more appropriate. Finally, while there are commonly used evaluation frameworks relevant to health care, these will need to be adapted on a case-by-case basis to a tailored training approach. This article will describe models and frameworks addressing the processes involved in developing, implementing, and evaluating customized behavioral safety skills training. Preliminary findings from an actual quality improvement initiative delivered to a long-term care facility in Ontario, Canada will be presented and used as a basis to discuss where theory and actual experience converge and diverge. Successful results include the development of a replicable and theory-grounded customization process along with demonstrated short-term staff-level improvements; however, challenges remain in terms of evaluating organizational-level impact, sustainability, and resident/patient-level outcomes.

items.title: Ethical decision-making for large language model use: a six-step model for mental health professionals.
items.authors: Fulmer R, Xiong Y, Zhai Y, Lee J, Nkya G, Naugle R.

sections.text: This article presents a six-step ethical decision-making model for mental health professionals confronted with ethical concerns arising when clients use large language models (LLMs) for mental health support. LLMs may introduce ethical problems that existing decision-making models were not designed to address. To provide guidance, we synthesized two bodies of research, the first concerning ethical risks posed by LLM use, and the second about existing decision-making models, to create a new model designed specifically for LLM and AI-related ethical issues. Our model addresses AI-specific phenomena such as deceptive empathy, algorithmic bias, digital attachment, and diffuse accountability structures. We propose this model as a conceptual foundation and encourage its ongoing refinement as AI continues to evolve.

items.title: The mediating role of perceived stress between the job demand-control-support model and occupational fatigue among operating room nurses: a multi-Center cross-sectional study.
items.authors: Qian W, Wu L, Wang X.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: Operating room nurses work long-term in high-intensity, high-risk environments and suffer from a high prevalence of occupational fatigue, which seriously affects their physical and mental health as well as patient safety. Based on the Job Demand-Control-Support (JDCS) model, this study aimed to examine the mediating role of perceived stress between the dimensions of the JDCS model and occupational fatigue-including acute fatigue, chronic fatigue, and inter-shift recovery-among operating room nurses.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This multi-center cross-sectional study was conducted from August to September 2026, enrolling 1,122 operating room nurses from 9 tertiary Grade-A hospitals in eastern, central, and western China. A general information questionnaire, the Occupational Fatigue Exhaustion Recovery Scale, the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-10), and the Job Content Questionnaire (JCQ) were administered. SPSS 25.0 was used for descriptive statistics, difference analysis, correlation analysis, and hierarchical multiple regression; AMOS 21.0 was used to construct a structural equation model, and the bias-corrected Bootstrap method was employed to test mediating effects.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The scores of acute fatigue, chronic fatigue, and inter-shift recovery among operating room nurses were 45.55 ± 18.77, 44.13 ± 17.89, and 56.27 ± 17.83, respectively, indicating an overall moderate level of occupational fatigue. The perceived stress score was 21.01 ± 5.24; job demand was 36.44 ± 4.80; job control was 71.54 ± 18.07; and social support was 24.02 ± 6.61. Hierarchical regression showed that, after controlling for demographic and work characteristics, job demand, job control, and social support remained independent correlates of all three outcomes (acute fatigue model R ^2 = 0.460, chronic fatigue R ^2 = 0.305, inter-shift recovery R ^2 = 0.353). The structural equation model showed that job demand positively predicted perceived stress ( β  = 0.182, p  < 0.001), while job control ( β  = -0.251, p  = 0.033) and social support ( β  = -0.168, p  = 0.040) negatively predicted perceived stress. Perceived stress positively predicted acute fatigue ( β  = 0.336, p  < 0.001) and chronic fatigue ( β  = 0.209, p  < 0.001), and negatively predicted inter-shift recovery ( β  = -0.134, p  = 0.029). Bootstrap tests indicated that perceived stress played a significant partial mediating role between job demand, job control, and social support and the outcomes of acute fatigue, chronic fatigue, and inter-shift recovery, although the indirect effects were small in magnitude (proportion mediated 3.41-17.35%).

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Occupational fatigue among operating room nurses in 9 tertiary Grade-A hospitals is at a moderate level, and inter-shift recovery needs improvement. Perceived stress acted as a mediating variable linking JDCS dimensions to occupational fatigue, although the mediating effects were modest in magnitude. Nursing managers can improve occupational fatigue and recovery among operating room nurses by reducing unreasonable job demands, enhancing job control, strengthening social support, and alleviating perceived stress.

items.title: Impact of cognitive reserve on stress, affect, and general mental health in the rural population of Rajasthan - A cross-sectional study.
items.authors: Mehta NA, Joshi P, Gautam S, Prasad J.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Cognitive reserve (CR) refers to the accumulation of cognitive capacities developed over a lifetime through one's life experiences.

sections.heading: Aim
sections.text: To examine the impact of CR on perceived stress, negative affect, and general mental health in the rural population in Rajasthan.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A total of 158 rural adults (aged 20-60 years) from Rajasthan (India) formed the sample. Cognitive impairment was screened using the Hindi Mini-Mental Status Examination (HVMMSE). Cognitive Reserve Index questionnaire (CRIq), Perceived Stress Scale-10 (PSS-10), Positive and Negative Affect Scale (PANAS), and General Health Questionnaire-12 (GHQ-12) were used to assess the variables.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The findings revealed a negative correlation between CR and adverse mental health outcomes (lower perceived stress, reduced negative affect, and better mental health). However, the effect size of CR on these variables was modest.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: The study highlights the protective role of CR against stress, negative affect, and poor mental health while underscoring gender-based disparities in CR.
